subject: 01-digital-logic
question_title: States unreachable from the initial register state
question_text: A synchronous circuit has three D flip-flops with common clock. Q1 feeds D2, Q2 feeds D3, and Q2 XOR Q3 feeds D1 through the feedback gate. State Si denotes the binary value i of Q1Q2Q3, so S0=000,...,S7=111. Starting at S4, identify all unreachable states.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
The next-state equations are (Q1,Q2,Q3)→(Q2 XOR Q3,Q1,Q2). Begin with S4=100 and repeatedly apply them. The successive states are S4=100, S2=010, S5=101, S6=110, S7=111, S3=011, S1=001, and then S4=100 again.

Once a deterministic state repeats, its subsequent trajectory repeats too; there is no input capable of taking a different branch. Therefore the reachable set is exactly {S1,S2,S3,S4,S5,S6,S7}, including the initial state itself at time zero. The only member of the eight-state space not visited is S0=000. It is unreachable from S4, although it is a perfectly valid state and would remain at zero forever if chosen as an initial state.

One can verify the exclusion algebraically. If the next state were 000, then new Q2=old Q1=0 and new Q3=old Q2=0. New Q1=old Q2 XOR old Q3=0 then forces old Q3=0. Thus only 000 can transition to 000; no nonzero state can enter it. The enumerated seven-state cycle proves that no additional state is excluded. GFG labels this subpart separately as question 73, but it is part (b) of original question 24 and shares that question's circuit and five-mark group allocation.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_title: CPU overhead of continuous DMA transfers
question_text: A 50 MHz processor uses DMA for a disk transferring 2000 Kbytes/s continuously. The average DMA block is 4 Kbytes. Each transfer needs 1000 processor cycles for setup and 500 processor cycles for its completion interrupt. What fraction of CPU time is consumed by disk handling?
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
First count transfers rather than bytes: 2000 Kbytes/s divided by 4 Kbytes/transfer is 500 transfers/s. The same meaning of K occurs in both quantities and cancels, so decimal versus binary K does not change this rate.

The processor performs 1000+500=1500 cycles of administrative work for every transfer. At 500 transfers/s this costs 750,000 CPU cycles/s. A 50 MHz processor supplies 50,000,000 cycles/s, so the fraction used is 750,000/50,000,000=0.015, or 1.5 percent.

An equivalent time calculation checks the units. Each processor cycle lasts 1/(50×10^6) s=20 ns. Setup takes 20 microseconds and the completion handler takes 10 microseconds, totaling 30 microseconds per transfer. Transferring 4K bytes at 2000K bytes/s takes 0.002 s=2 milliseconds; 30 microseconds/2 milliseconds again equals 0.015. The transfer uses DMA, so the CPU is not charged for executing an instruction per byte. The calculation counts only the specified setup and completion overhead; additional bus-contention stalls, queuing effects, or other driver costs are not given and should not be invented. subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_title: Choosing hierarchy sizes with model caveats
question_text: A three-level hierarchy has level-1 access time 50 ns/byte and options 8KB (hit .80), 16KB (.90), 64KB (.95); level-2 access time 200 ns/byte and options 4MB (hit .98), 16MB (.99), 64MB (.995); level 3 has access time 5 microseconds/byte, size 250MB, hit 1.0. Use the GFG table; GateForum has inconsistent duplicated tables, KB/MB units and 250/260MB labels. The question does not explicitly state whether lower-level access times include earlier failed probes. Choose minimum level-1 and level-2 sizes giving average access time strictly below 100 ns.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
If the tabulated times are complete service times for a hit at the corresponding level, and h2 is conditional on missing level 1, then T=h1·50+(1−h1)h2·200+(1−h1)(1−h2)·5000. Try the smallest options first: h1=.80 and h2=.98. Their mutually exclusive outcome probabilities are .80, .196, and .004, summing to one. Hence T=40+39.2+20=99.2 ns, strictly below 100. Since 8KB and 4MB are individually the smallest listed sizes, this pair is componentwise minimal in that model.

A different standard convention treats 50,200,5000 as incremental sequential probe times. Then every access pays 50, every L1 miss pays another 200, and a miss in both pays another 5000: Tseq=50+(1−h1)[200+(1−h2)5000]. The same 8KB/4MB pair gives 110 ns and fails. At 8KB, increasing L2 to 16MB gives exactly 100 ns, still failing the strict inequality; 64MB gives 95 ns. At 16KB, the smallest L2=4MB already gives 80 ns. Thus the nondominated feasible pairs in the sequential model are (8KB,64MB) and (16KB,4MB); neither is smaller in both coordinates. Minimizing total installed bytes selects (16KB,4MB), whereas minimizing L1 first selects (8KB,64MB).

Therefore the familiar 8KB/4MB answer requires the complete-service-time interpretation. Without specifying the timing convention, the literal question has no single model-independent answer. The lower-level hit ratio is also taken as conditional, not as an additional unconditional probability.
derived_answer: Complete-service-time model: 8KB L1 and 4MB L2 (99.2 ns). Sequential probing gives different feasible minima; see solution.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_title: Average access time for selected hierarchy
question_text: A three-level hierarchy has level-1 access time 50 ns/byte and options 8KB (hit .80), 16KB (.90), 64KB (.95); level-2 access time 200 ns/byte and options 4MB (hit .98), 16MB (.99), 64MB (.995); level 3 has access time 5 microseconds/byte, size 250MB, hit 1.0. The question does not explicitly state whether lower-level access times include earlier failed probes. Calculate the average time for the sizes selected to satisfy the strict 100 ns bound.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
For the complete-service-time interpretation, select the smallest listed capacities, L1=8KB and L2=4MB. An access hits L1 with probability .80 and takes 50 ns. It misses L1 and hits L2 with probability .20×.98=.196 and takes 200 ns. It misses both with probability .20×.02=.004 and takes 5000 ns. The mean is therefore .80×50+.196×200+.004×5000=40+39.2+20=99.2 ns per byte. This is 0.8 ns below the required bound. Notice that even the rare .4 percent accesses to level 3 contribute 20 ns to the mean.

This calculation uses exclusive end-to-end outcomes. If the table instead lists incremental sequential access times, earlier failed probes must also be charged: 50+.20×200+.004×5000=110 ns for these same capacities, so they would not be a valid choice. In that model, the (16KB,4MB) pair gives 50+.10×200+(.10×.02)×5000=80 ns. The alternative nondominated (8KB,64MB) pair gives 50+.20×200+(.20×.005)×5000=95 ns. The (8KB,16MB) pair gives exactly 100 ns, which is excluded by “less than”.

Thus report 99.2 ns together with its timing assumption, rather than presenting it as a verified official value. Both table-unit defects in GateForum and the unstated timing convention should remain visible to students; neither justifies inventing an official answer key.
derived_answer: 99.2 ns in the complete-service-time model; sequential alternatives are 80 ns for 16KB/4MB or 95 ns for 8KB/64MB.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_text: Relations are USERS(User#,UserName,HomeTown), BOOKS(Book#,BookTitle,AuthorName), and ISSUED(Book#,User#,Date). Natural joins match the identically named key attributes. Explain in one English sentence the query σ_User#=6(π_User#,BookTitle((USERS ⋈ ISSUED) ⋈ BOOKS)). This paraphrase uses GFG's legible relational operators; GateForum's reproduction drops join symbols and degrades projection typography.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
One-sentence answer: It returns user number 6 together with the titles of books recorded as issued to that user.

To see why, USERS ⋈ ISSUED first connects each issue record with the user whose User# matches. Joining this result with BOOKS on Book# adds the associated BookTitle and AuthorName. The projection π_User#,BookTitle retains just the user identifier and title, discarding names, dates, book identifiers and author names. Finally σ_User#=6 keeps only rows whose user identifier is 6.

Selection occurs after projection here without losing its input attribute, because User# is explicitly retained. It could equivalently be pushed earlier to restrict the user or issue records before the joins. Under ordinary set-based relational algebra, projection removes duplicate pairs: borrowing the same titled book more than once does not produce multiple identical (6,title) rows, and distinct books with the same title also collapse at this projection. No return-date or current-loan condition exists in the schema, so “recorded as issued” is more precise than claiming these are necessarily the user's currently unreturned books. The query yields titles with the fixed identifier 6, not a count of loans, author names, or all users who borrowed the same books.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_title: Interpreting authors read by a hometown group
question_text: Relations are USERS(User#,UserName,HomeTown), BOOKS(Book#,BookTitle,AuthorName), and ISSUED(Book#,User#,Date). Natural joins match the identically named key attributes. Explain in one English sentence the query π_AuthorName(BOOKS ⋈ σ_HomeTown='Delhi'(USERS ⋈ ISSUED)). Use the projection and natural-join symbols visible in GFG; GateForum misprints/degrades these operators.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
One-sentence answer: It returns the names of authors having at least one book recorded as issued to a user whose hometown is Delhi.

The inner natural join USERS ⋈ ISSUED matches each issue to its borrower through User#. Selecting HomeTown='Delhi' retains issue records belonging to Delhi users; the condition describes the borrower's hometown, not the author's residence or the book's publication place. The join with BOOKS matches Book# and adds the author of each surviving issued book. Projection onto AuthorName then discards every other attribute.

Under set semantics each distinct author name appears once, even if several Delhi users borrowed that author's books or one user borrowed several such books. The condition is existential: one qualifying issue suffices. It does not require that all books by the author have been issued, that every Delhi user has read the author, or that the author is popular by any numerical threshold. Likewise nothing in the given schema tests whether a book has since been returned. If no Delhi user has any issue record, the result is empty. Two different people who happen to share AuthorName are not distinguished by this schema and projection; the result is a set of names rather than necessarily unique real-world author identities. GateForum's apparent σ before AuthorName would not be a well-formed selection predicate; the GFG π supplies the coherent reading.
derived_answer: Names of authors with at least one book issued to a Delhi-hometown user.

question_text: Which standard representation permits O(1) concatenation: singly linked, doubly linked, circular doubly linked, or array list?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.

question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: An N-bit adder uses 4-bit 74181 ALUs and 4-bit 74182 carry generators, with N divisible by 4. What is best asymptotic addition delay?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: A four-way carry generator combines propagate/generate information for four lower-level groups. Cascading these in a balanced hierarchy reduces the number of groups by a factor of four per level. Therefore carry information traverses O(log₄ N)=O(log N) levels, followed by constant local sum-generation work. B is the best bounded-fan-in architecture among the choices. A serial chain would take linear time, but is not the best organization; constant delay would require unbounded fan-in or a different physical model.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: On all integers define n*m=max (n, m). Is this a monoid, Abelian group, group, or none?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: Maximum is associative, commutative and closed on integers. A monoid additionally needs an identity e satisfying max (e, n)=n for every integer n. That would require e≤n for every integer, but no least integer exists: choose n=e−1 to contradict it. Thus there is no identity and hence no group structure either, giving D. On a set with an added−∞ element, that element would be an identity, but it is not an integer in the stated domain.

question_text: Hasse chains are f<e<b<a, f<g<a, f<d<c<a, with no further covers. How many complements does e have?

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: Over{a, b}, which is uncountable: all finite strings, all languages, regular languages, or Turing-recognizable languages?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: Finite strings can be enumerated by length and lexicographic order, so Σ* is countably infinite. All languages form its power set P(Σ*), which is uncountable by Cantor’s theorem. In contrast, finite automata and Turing machines each have finite descriptions over a finite alphabet, so there are only countably many of either and hence only countably many languages they describe. Thus B. The distinction is between elements that are strings and arbitrary sets of those strings.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: A page reference always repeats the previous page, is likely among recently used pages, always hits resident memory, or always faults.
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: Temporal locality is the tendency to reuse recently accessed data or instructions, for example within a loop. Hence the next page reference is likely to be among a recent working set, B. This is a statistical tendency, not an absolute guarantee. A program can move to a new phase and access a different page, and whether that page is resident depends on available memory and replacement history. Thus the three statements containing always are too strong.

question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: The handler’s action depends on the event. An ordinary completed-I/O interrupt may simply update device state and return, while a fault or trap requiring an unavailable resource may block the current process and allow another to run. Thus neither always blocking nor always resuming is a general rule. D correctly expresses a possible outcome. This uses interrupt broadly enough to include synchronous traps/faults; a narrow device-only definition would need more careful distinctions about why the interrupted process blocks.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: Thrashing reduces page I/O, decreases multiprogramming by definition, implies excessive page I/O, or improves performance?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: Thrashing occurs when processes repeatedly fault because their active working sets do not fit in available frames. The system spends excessive time moving pages rather than executing useful instructions, so C describes it. It increases rather than reduces paging traffic and degrades performance. Reducing the degree of multiprogramming may be a remedy, but is not automatically the meaning or inevitable direct effect of thrashing, so B confuses response with condition.

solution: A dirty bit records whether a page has been modified since its backing-store copy was synchronized. question_text: T(1)=1 and T(n)=2T(floor (n/2))+sqrt (n) for n≥2. Choose O(sqrt n), O(n), O(log n), none.

solution: At recursion depth j there are roughly 2^j subproblems of size n/2^j. Their combined nonrecursive work is sqrt (n)·2^(j/2), increasing geometrically toward the leaves. Summing through depth about log 2 n gives O(n), and there are Θ(n) leaves each contributing constant work, providing Ω(n). Hence T(n)=Θ(n), so B. Equivalently the Master theorem has n^(log 2 2)=n and toll n^(1/2), which is polynomially smaller; rounding does not change the asymptotic order.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text: A priority queue is used to implement a LIFO stack. PUSH inserts an item with a chosen integer key; POP deletes the minimum. Should keys be nonincreasing, nondecreasing, strictly increasing, or strictly decreasing?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: The newest live item must have the smallest key so it is returned first. Assign successively decreasing keys, for example 0, −1, −2, …; then delete-min exactly follows last-in-first-out order. Strict decrease prevents ties whose unspecified resolution could return an older item. Thus D is the standard sufficient choice. A merely nonincreasing sequence permits equal keys and does not guarantee LIFO without an extra tie rule. Keys need only outrank still-live items, so global decrease is a simple implementation policy rather than the only possible schedule-aware assignment.
derived_answer: D as the sufficient unambiguous scheme

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text: For expression prefix (a*b)*c op…where op is+, *, or exponentiation, which operators permit the accumulated product to remain in one register?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.

If op is+or*, ordinary precedence and left associativity allow completing the multiplication by c before moving to the following operation; the accumulator can be reused without spilling a*b. If op is exponentiation, the c-power subexpression binds more tightly and normally must be computed before multiplying by the held a*b, creating a second live intermediate. Thus A in the stated compiler-evaluation model. question_text: Vertices 1…100 are adjacent when their difference is 8 or12. Count connected components among 8, 4, 12, 25.
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: Every allowed difference is divisible by 4, so a path preserves residue modulo 4. There are at least four components. Each residue class contains 25 vertices; after rescaling by 4, its edges connect indices differing by 2 or3. These 25 indices form a connected graph: all odd indices connect by 2, all even indices connect by 2, and the edge 1–4 of difference 3 joins the two chains. Hence each residue class is one component, proving exactly four, B. The boundary argument is necessary; a gcd observation alone would only prove the lower bound for a finite interval.

question_text: Three processes each may require two units of one resource. Minimum units guaranteeing no allocation deadlock among 3, 5, 4, 6?

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_title: A process signals instead of waiting
question_text: Nine processes repeat P(mutex);critical section;V(mutex). A tenth replaces its initial P by V. What maximum number can be inside simultaneously?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: The faulty process never consumes a permit when entering and adds permits both before entering and after leaving. With a counting semaphore, it can complete enough loops to accumulate at least nine permits while the others wait to run. Then schedule all nine correct processes through P and pause each inside its critical section. Finally let the faulty process enter too: all ten are inside. Ten is the absolute upper bound because only ten processes exist, so it is attained. Even a saturating binary semaphore can be repeatedly reopened by the faulty process to admit more peers before they leave. Thus D.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: An 8085 must drive a one-bit output port at I/O address FF hexadecimal through a D flip-flop. The transferred bit is D3, and the output must clear at power-on. Using exactly one ten-input NAND gate, one inverter and one D flip-flop, give the interface circuit. State clock/reset polarities explicitly.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
The eight-bit I/O address FFH is all ones. In an 8085 I/O cycle, that address is duplicated on the high address bus A15…A8, so these eight nonmultiplexed lines can be decoded without adding an address latch. Do not use AD7…AD0 directly throughout the write: those pins carry the data during the data phase.

Let /WR denote the active-low write strobe and IO/M=1 denote an I/O cycle. Use the one inverter to form W=NOT(/WR). The ten-input NAND receives A15,A14,…,A8,IO/M,W. Its output is
CLK = NOT(A15·A14·…·A8·IO/M·W).

A complete connection list is:
8085 D3 → D input of the flip-flop.
A15…A8, IO/M, NOT(/WR) → the ten NAND inputs.
NAND output → positive-edge-triggered CLK.
RESET OUT → active-high asynchronous CLEAR.
Q → the one-bit output.
Any asynchronous preset input is tied inactive.

For FFH on an I/O write, CLK goes low while /WR is asserted and rises when that write ends. The positive edge captures D3 while the data is valid. For another port, a memory cycle, or a nonwrite cycle, at least one NAND input is zero and the clock remains high. Asynchronous clearing makes Q=0 during the power-on reset independently of clock activity.

The flip-flop's clear polarity matters. The above netlist chooses an active-high CLEAR so the 8085's active-high RESET OUT connects directly. With an active-low /CLR device instead, connect the same active-low power-on /RESET IN net that resets the CPU to /CLR. Do not connect RESET OUT directly to /CLR and do not silently use a second inverter. The edge and reset assumptions are explicit because the question does not specify a particular flip-flop part. This is an ideal bus-timing design, assuming normal setup/hold timing and no wait-state or reset anomaly.
derived_answer: D←D3; CLK←NAND(A15,…,A8,IO/M,NOT(/WR)); asynchronous clear from reset; Q is the port output.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: An 8085 must drive a one-bit output port at I/O address FF hexadecimal through a D flip-flop. The transferred bit is D3, and the output must clear at power-on. Write an 8085 program producing equal ON and OFF intervals of seven bus/machine cycles each.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
Only accumulator bit 3 affects this one-bit port. Complementing the entire accumulator is therefore enough to toggle the output: bit 3 alternates between 0 and 1. One program is

        MVI A,00H
LOOP:   CMA
        OUT FFH
        JMP LOOP

CMA takes one machine cycle, OUT takes three, and an unconditional JMP takes three. Between the end of one OUT and the end of the next OUT, the processor executes JMP, CMA and OUT. The total is 3+1+3=7 machine cycles. The same instruction path is used whether D3 is changing from 0 to 1 or from 1 to 0, so both steady-state half-periods are equal. At the FFH output port, values FFH and 00H alternate, but only their D3 bits are stored.

The initialization MVI is outside the loop and does not contribute to repeated periods. Power-on clearing ensures the initial output is low; the interval from reset release to the very first transition need not equal a later half-period. Interrupts and inserted wait states must be absent if exact timing is required.

Here “bus cycles” is interpreted as the 8085 machine-cycle count, not seven clock T-states. The instructions take 4+10+10=24 T-states in a normal execution, so a complete square-wave period is 14 machine cycles, or 48 T-states. Counting instruction bytes or taking “7” as seven T-states would give the wrong timing model.
derived_answer: MVI A,00H; LOOP: CMA; OUT FFH; JMP LOOP. Each steady-state half-period is 1+3+3=7 machine cycles.

question_text: The vertices are the n² integer lattice points (x,y), 1≤x,y≤n, n≥2. Distinct vertices are adjacent when BOTH |x1−x2|≤1 and |y1−y2|≤1; an edge has Euclidean length sqrt((x1−x2)²+(y1−y2)²). This is the GateForum p11 adjacency, including the second-coordinate bound omitted in GFG. Find the minimum spanning-tree weight.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
There are n² vertices, so every spanning tree has exactly n²−1 edges. Distinct integer lattice points are at distance at least 1; hence every spanning tree has weight at least n²−1.

This bound is achievable without using any diagonals. In each row, connect its n vertices consecutively with n−1 horizontal unit edges. This uses n(n−1) edges and leaves n connected row paths. Connect consecutive rows by vertical unit edges along the first column, using n−1 more edges. The result is connected and has n(n−1)+(n−1)=n²−1 edges; equivalently, joining the disjoint row trees by a path cannot create a cycle. Its weight is exactly n²−1, matching the lower bound.

For n=2 this construction has three unit edges and weight 3. Using a diagonal would replace a unit edge by one of length √2 and cannot improve the minimum.

The source variant matters for the companion maximum-weight question: GFG prints only |x1−x2|≤1, permitting long changes in y. For this minimum, however, the same answer remains valid under that literal variant. All distinct vertices are still at least unit distance apart, and the unit-edge construction is still allowed. Thus this particular answer is robust even though the reproduced graph definitions differ.

question_text: The vertices are the n² integer lattice points (x,y), 1≤x,y≤n, n≥2. Find the maximum spanning-tree weight; also distinguish the literal GFG graph that constrains only |x1−x2|≤1.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
In the stated king-move grid, every edge is either horizontal/vertical with weight 1 or diagonal with weight √2. We therefore want as many diagonal edges as a spanning tree can contain.

Color vertex (x,y) by the parity of x+y. A diagonal changes both coordinates by one, so it preserves this parity; a horizontal or vertical edge changes it. Both parity classes are nonempty for n≥2. A connected spanning tree must consequently include at least one unit edge to join the two classes. Since it has n²−1 edges in total, its weight is at most (n²−2)√2+1.

To attain the bound, observe that the diagonal-only graph has exactly two connected components, one of each parity. Here is a constructive connectivity argument. Repeatedly use an upward diagonal to reduce y until reaching the first row; at a side boundary choose the inward direction, always possible because n≥2. On the first row, vertices of a fixed parity can move two columns at a time through a vertex of the second row. Thus all vertices of each parity are connected by diagonals. Take a spanning tree inside each diagonal component. Together they use n²−2 diagonal edges. Add any unit edge between the components. This produces a spanning tree attaining the upper bound.

For n=2 the two diagonals, joined by one side, have weight 2√2+1. That is the answer to GateForum's full adjacency rule. Under GFG's literal omission of the y-bound, longer edges are allowed when n≥3. Its maximum is instead

(2n−2)√(1+(n−1)²) + (n−1) + nΣ_(j=2)^(n−1)√(1+max(j−1,n−j)²).

Here is a separate optimality proof for that literal graph. Call vertices on y=1 or y=n boundary vertices. For each interior vertex at row j, select an edge to a farthest boundary row in an adjacent column. Such a column always exists for n≥2. Its length is √(1+max(j−1,n−j)²), a maximum edge across the cut isolating that vertex. Add these edges while each interior vertex is still isolated; all chosen parents are boundary vertices, so no cycle arises. By the maximum-spanning-tree cut property, each addition is safe.

Next add all 2n−2 boundary diagonals with |dx|=1 and |dy|=n−1. They are globally maximum edges, each of length √(1+(n−1)²), and form two disjoint alternating-row paths on the 2n boundary vertices. Interior attachments do not join those paths. Finally join them by a same-column edge from y=1 to y=n, of length n−1. Every competing cross-component edge with an interior endpoint is at most √(1+(n−2)²)<n−1 for n≥3. Remaining boundary cross-edges have length at most n−1, so this last edge is also cut-safe. At n=2 there are no interior vertices and the bridge length is 1.

The safe selections form a spanning tree and give the displayed sum: n equal-length interior attachments for each row j, 2n−2 boundary diagonals, and one bridge. Thus both materially different printed graphs have an explicit maximum and a proof, rather than silently restoring a bound in GFG.

subject: 03-programming-in-c
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
Pass by value gives every call its own local x, but all calls still share the same global z. It is important not to copy z into each activation or to overwrite a caller's x with its child's final x.

On descent, no assignment z:=x+10 has executed yet: it comes after the recursive call. Therefore z stays 10 while the successive calls enter with x=10,20,30,40,50. The calls entering with 10,20,30,40 first update their local x to 20,30,40,50 respectively. The final call enters with x=50; because 50≤40 is false, it immediately returns.

Now unwind the suspended calls:
Entered x=40, saved updated x=50: assign z=60.
Entered x=30, saved updated x=40: assign z=50.
Entered x=20, saved updated x=30: assign z=40.
Entered x=10, saved updated x=20: assign z=30.

The outer call is last to write the shared global, so writeln(z) prints 30. The temporary value 60 produced by the deepest active body is not the final answer. Also, x=40 does execute its body, because both visual sources show ≤40 rather than <40. The individual marks for this nested leaf are not printed; they are left unknown rather than assigning an invented share of the original group's marks.

solution:
The main program calls recur(z), so its reference parameter x is another name for the global variable z. Passing that reference onward as recur(x) keeps the same alias in every activation. There are not separate saved integer values of x in the suspended calls.

Initially x=z=10. The first body executes x:=x+z, doubling the shared variable to 20. The next call doubles it to 40. Because the guard is x≤40, the call seeing 40 also executes the body and doubles it to 80. The next call sees 80 and returns immediately. On unwinding, every z:=x+10 reads the current shared value, because x aliases z. The three pending assignments make the values 80→90→100→110. The program consequently prints 110.

It would be incorrect to use the descent values 10,20,40 as saved local copies during unwinding: that is pass-by-value behavior. It would also be incorrect to stop at 80, since the three assignments following recursive calls still have to execute. The example shows why mutation of a reference argument can interact unexpectedly with a global variable naming the same storage location.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text:
Use the GFG grammar with start symbol S:
S → bSe | PQR
P → bPc | ε
Q → cQd | ε
R → dRe | ε.
Terminals are b,c,d,e. Generated words are b^i c^j d^k e^m with nonnegative integer exponents. GateForum instead prints S→bSc and mistakenly gives nonpositive exponents; those literal variants must be distinguished.
What condition on i,j,k,m characterizes the generated language?
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
Let t be the number of uses of S→bSe before S→PQR. Let p,q,r be the numbers of recursive productions used by P,Q,R. Their contributions are P⇒b^p c^p, Q⇒c^q d^q and R⇒d^r e^r. Combining them with the outer b/e pairs gives

i=t+p,  j=p+q,  k=q+r,  m=r+t,
where t,p,q,r are nonnegative integers. Adding opposite equations yields the necessary relation i+k=j+m.

To prove sufficiency, assume all four exponents are nonnegative and i+k=j+m. Choose any integer t satisfying max(0,i−j)≤t≤min(i,m), and put p=i−t, q=j−i+t, r=m−t. These parameters are nonnegative and reproduce every exponent, including k=j−i+m. Such a t always exists: i−j≤m follows from k≥0, while i−j≤i follows from j≥0. Thus the equality, together with nonnegativity, is also sufficient.

GateForum's visibly different rule S→bSc cannot silently be substituted. Its full generated form is b^(t+p)c^(p+q)d^(q+r)e^r c^t, with a trailing block of c symbols after the d/e blocks. For example S⇒bSc⇒bPQRc⇒bcdc is possible, contradicting that reproduction's claim that every generated word is in b*c*d*e*. Restricting to words of the claimed block form forces either t=0, or q=r=0 so no d/e lies before the final c. The t=0 case gives i=p,j=p+q,k=q+r,m=r, hence i+k=j+m and j≥i. The other case gives only b^i c^i, already included in that subset. Thus the block-form subset has that extra inequality, but it is not the whole literal GateForum language. The word be belongs to GFG but not GateForum.

Finally, GateForum's printed i,j,k,m≤0 is inconsistent with arbitrary nonempty strings of repeated terminals. Taken literally as string exponents, only zero exponents are meaningful, leaving ε; the language intended by the grammar is not that singleton. This solution uses nonnegative counts, as explicitly printed in GFG, and discloses both source differences.
derived_answer: For GFG: i,j,k,m≥0 and i+k=j+m. GateForum literal S→bSc also generates words outside b*c*d*e*; its block-form subset additionally requires j≥i.

question_text: A hash table has n≥1 buckets, uses external chaining, and is initially empty. K distinct keys are inserted. Each key hashes uniformly to one of the n buckets. Under the standard additional assumption that different keys hash independently, find the probability that bucket 1 is empty after K insertions.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
A single inserted key avoids bucket 1 with probability (n−1)/n=1−1/n. Bucket 1 is empty after K insertions exactly when every one of those K keys avoids it. Under independent hashing, multiply the K probabilities to obtain

P(bucket 1 empty) = (1−1/n)^K.

The table may have collisions in other buckets; they do not affect this event. External chaining allows arbitrarily many keys in a bucket, so K need not be at most n. For K=0 the probability is 1, including the n=1 case, by the empty-product convention. For n=1 and K≥1 it is 0, because the only bucket must receive every key. For n=2,K=3 it is (1/2)^3=1/8.

The independence qualification is substantive. The source supplies the uniform probability for any individual key, but marginal uniformity alone is not enough to multiply events. For example, choose one uniformly random bucket U and send all keys to U. Every key is marginally uniform, yet bucket 1 remains empty with probability 1−1/n for every K≥1, rather than (1−1/n)^K. The displayed answer uses the usual independent-uniform hashing model and is not claimed under that correlated alternative.

question_text: A hash table has n≥1 buckets, uses external chaining, and is initially empty. K distinct keys are inserted. Each key hashes uniformly to one of the n buckets. Under the standard additional assumption that different keys hash independently, find the probability that none of the K insertions causes a collision.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
After j collision-free insertions, exactly j buckets are occupied. Conditional on that event, the next independently hashed key must choose one of the n−j empty buckets, which has probability (n−j)/n. Multiplying from j=0 through K−1 gives

P(no collision in K insertions)
= 1·(n−1)/n·(n−2)/n·…·(n−K+1)/n
= n! / ((n−K)! n^K), for 0≤K≤n.

For K>n the probability is zero by the pigeonhole principle. Do not extend the factorial formula to a negative factorial. At K=0, the empty product is 1; at K=1, no collision is possible and the result is also 1. For n=3,K=2 it is 2/3, because only the second key can cause the first collision.

An equivalent counting argument considers n^K equally likely ordered bucket-choice sequences. Collision-free choices are injective assignments of the K ordered keys to the n buckets, numbering n(n−1)…(n−K+1). The keys are distinct, but that does not make their bucket values distinct automatically.

This derivation needs independent uniform hashing, not just equal marginal bucket probabilities. Under the correlated scheme that sends every key to one common randomly chosen bucket, the probability is already zero at K=2 despite uniform marginals. That source-model limitation is stated explicitly rather than hidden in the multiplication.

The event consists of two parts: the first K−1 insertions are collision-free, and the Kth key hits one of their occupied buckets. Given the first part, there are exactly K−1 occupied buckets, so the conditional probability of the second part is (K−1)/n.

For 2≤K≤n+1, the requested probability is therefore

[n(n−1)…(n−K+2)/n^(K−1)]·(K−1)/n
= n!(K−1) / ((n−K+1)! n^K).

The upper endpoint n+1 is legitimate: the first n keys could fill all n buckets without a collision, after which the next key certainly collides. Its probability is n!/n^n. For K=1 the event is impossible because an empty table has no occupied bucket. For K>n+1, a first collision must already have happened, so the probability is also zero.

As a check, write p_j for the probability of no collision after j insertions. Then P(first at K)=p_(K−1)−p_K. Summing from K=2 to n+1 telescopes to p_1−p_(n+1)=1, as required. question_title: Count injections into a larger set
question_text: Let F be all one-to-one functions from {1,…,n} to {1,…,m}, where m≥n≥1. How many functions belong to F?
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
Choose the values of the function in domain order. There are m choices for f(1). Once it is chosen, injectivity excludes that value for f(2), leaving m−1 choices. In general f(i) has m−i+1 choices after the preceding i−1 images have been fixed. The multiplication principle gives

|F| = m(m−1)…(m−n+1) = m!/(m−n)!.

Another way is to choose the n-element image set, in C(m,n) ways, then assign its distinct members to the n labelled domain elements, in n! ways. Hence |F|=C(m,n)n!, the same result.

The distinction between a function and an image set matters: C(m,n) alone discards the order in which the n selected values are assigned to 1,…,n. For n=2,m=3, the image set {1,2} supplies both f(1)=1,f(2)=2 and f(1)=2,f(2)=1. There are six injections overall, not three. At n=1 the answer is m, and at m=n it is n!, the number of permutations, providing simple boundary checks.

question_title: Count injections whose image contains one
question_text: Let F be all one-to-one functions from {1,…,n} to {1,…,m}, where m≥n≥1. How many f satisfy f(i)=1 for some domain element i?
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
Because f is one-to-one, the codomain value 1 can occur at exactly one domain position if it occurs at all. Choose that position i in n ways. The remaining n−1 domain elements must receive distinct values from the other m−1 codomain values, giving (m−1)!/(m−n)! assignments. Thus the total is

n·(m−1)!/(m−n)!.

There is no double-counting: each satisfying function has a unique preimage of 1, so it appears in exactly one of the n cases. Equivalently, choose its image set to contain 1 and n−1 other values, then order the n image values over the domain. This gives C(m−1,n−1)n!, equal to the first expression.

As a probability check, divide by all m!/(m−n)! injections. The fraction whose image contains a specified codomain value is n/m, consistent with an image set containing n out of m values symmetrically. At n=1 there is only one satisfying function, f(1)=1. At n=m every injection is a bijection, so all n! functions qualify. question_text: Let F be all one-to-one functions from {1,…,n} to {1,…,m}, where m≥n≥1. GFG asks for f(i)<f(j) for ALL 1≤i<j≤n; GateForum asks for this for SOME pair. Give the count for each printed variant.

GateForum prints an existential condition: there must be at least one pair i<j for which f(i)<f(j). Count its complement. Failure means f(i)≥f(j) for every i<j. Subtracting from all injections gives

m!/(m−n)! − C(m,n).

For n=2 the two numerical answers happen to coincide, which can conceal the wording discrepancy in small checks.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: Let R be a reflexive and transitive relation on a set A. Define E={(a,b):aRb and bRa}. Prove that E is an equivalence relation.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
We must check the three equivalence-relation axioms on the same set A.

Reflexivity: for every a∈A, reflexivity of R gives aRa. Both required directions in the definition of E are then the same true statement, so aEa.

Symmetry: if aEb, the definition supplies both aRb and bRa. Reversing their order immediately gives bEa. No symmetry assumption about R is needed; taking its mutual part creates symmetry.

Transitivity: suppose aEb and bEc. Then aRb and bRc, so transitivity of R yields aRc. We also have cRb and bRa, so another use of transitivity gives cRa. Both directions hold, establishing aEc.

Thus E is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, hence an equivalence relation. Its classes group elements that are mutually related by R. In a directed-reachability interpretation, R says one vertex can reach another, and E groups vertices that can reach each other in both directions.

The proof does not claim that R itself is symmetric or antisymmetric. A reflexive, transitive relation is a preorder and may relate distinct elements in both directions. Passing to E-classes is precisely how the companion part removes that possible failure of antisymmetry.
derived_answer: E is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

question_text: Let R be a reflexive and transitive relation on a set A. Define E={(a,b):aRb and bRa}. For E-classes C,D, define C≤D when there exist a∈C,b∈D with aRb. Prove that this gives a partial order on A/E.

Reflexivity: choose a∈C. Since aRa, the defining witness gives C≤C.

Antisymmetry: suppose C≤D and D≤C. Choose any a∈C,b∈D. Representative independence gives aRb from the first relation and bRa from the second. Hence aEb, so a and b have the same E-class and C=D. Antisymmetry is equality of classes, not necessarily equality of their individual representatives.

Transitivity: suppose C≤D and D≤H. Choose a∈C,b∈D,c∈H. Representative independence supplies aRb and bRc; transitivity of R yields aRc. Therefore C≤H.

All partial-order axioms hold. The preliminary representative step is essential when starting from existential witnesses: the witness b from C≤D and the witness b′ from D≤H might be different elements of D. Their E-equivalence supplies bRb′, which connects the two chains. Omitting that link would leave a gap in a direct transitivity proof. No total-order claim follows: two equivalence classes can be incomparable when neither direction of R holds between them.

question_text:
For positive integers n,m, consider the directly recursive, nonmemoized function
function F(n,m:integer):integer;
begin
  if (n<=0) or (m<=0) then F:=1
  else F:=F(n-1,m)+F(n,m-1)
end.
Use C(s,t)=C(s−1,t)+C(s−1,t−1).
Find F(n,2).
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
Start with m=1. The recurrence says F(n,1)=F(n−1,1)+F(n,0)=F(n−1,1)+1, and F(0,1)=1. Therefore F(n,1)=n+1.

Now use m=2. We get F(n,2)=F(n−1,2)+F(n,1)=F(n−1,2)+(n+1), with F(0,2)=1. Summing the increments from 1 through n gives

F(n,2)=1+Σ_(r=1)^n(r+1)
=1+n(n+1)/2+n
=(n+1)(n+2)/2.

This equals C(n+2,2), anticipating the general binomial formula. A direct induction check also works: the proposed formula for n−1 is n(n+1)/2; adding n+1 gives (n+1)(n+2)/2. The base n=0 gives 1 as required.

For n=1, F(1,2)=F(0,2)+F(1,1)=1+2=3, consistent with the formula. The offset matters: n(n+1)/2 would correspond to a different boundary condition and would incorrectly give 1 when n=1. Both axes in this program have value 1, not 0.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text: A size-balanced binary tree has, at every node, left and right subtree sizes differing by at most one. Node distance is the number of edges from the root, and tree height h is the greatest root-to-leaf distance. Prove by induction on h that a tree of height h has at least 2^h nodes.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
Use induction on the nonnegative height h. For h=0 the tree consists of the root, so N=1=2^0.

For h≥1, at least one child subtree has height h−1; otherwise no root-to-leaf path could have length h. Call that subtree T and let its size be s. By the induction hypothesis, s≥2^(h−1). The other child subtree has size t≥s−1, because the defining balance condition bounds the size difference by one. Empty subtrees are allowed and have size zero, so this also handles h=1.

Counting the root gives

N=1+s+t ≥1+s+(s−1)=2s ≥2^h.

This proves the assertion. We did not assume the two subtrees have equal height or that every level is full. Size balance is a statement about node counts, and the proof uses exactly that statement.

The bound is sharp. For h≥1, combine a minimum-size tree of height h−1, with 2^(h−1) nodes, and a perfect tree of height h−2, with 2^(h−1)−1 nodes, below a new root. Their sizes differ by one and their subtrees satisfy the same condition. The total is 2^h and the height is h. At h=1 the smaller subtree is empty. This construction also explains why the stronger bound 2^(h+1)−1 would be false: a size-balanced tree need not be perfect at its last level.
derived_answer: Every such tree has N≥2^h; the bound is attainable.

question_text: A size-balanced binary tree has, at every node, left and right subtree sizes differing by at most one. Node distance is the number of edges from the root, and tree height h is the greatest root-to-leaf distance. For h≥1, how many nodes are at distance h−1 from the root?

The level at distance h−1 is full, so it contains 2^(h−1) nodes. To justify fullness rather than assume it, first use the proved size bound: a size-balanced tree of height h has N≥2^h nodes.

For any node whose subtree has s nodes, its child sizes sum to s−1 and differ by at most one. Hence each child has at least floor((s−1)/2) nodes. Starting from N≥2^h, induction on depth shows that every node at depth d≤h−1 has subtree size at least 2^(h−d)−1. Indeed, a parent lower bound 2^(h−d)−1 gives each child at least 2^(h−d−1)−1.

In particular, at every depth d<h−1 this lower bound is at least 3. Such a subtree has both children nonempty. Beginning with one root, the node count therefore doubles at each step until depth h−1, giving exactly 2^(h−1) nodes there. The last level h may be only partly occupied, so this does not assert that the entire tree is perfect.

For h=1 the requested level is the root itself and the formula gives 1. For h=2 a smallest example has four nodes: its depth-1 level still has both children, while only one node need occur at depth 2. GFG explicitly states h≥1. GateForum visibly prints h≤1; under that literal restriction h=0 would ask for a negative distance, so the nonnegative-depth question uses the coherent GFG range and flags the typo.

question_text: In this question a B+-tree of order d has d to 2d key entries in each nonroot internal node, and an internal node with M keys has M+1 children. An internal root has 1 to 2d keys. All leaves are at equal edge-distance h from the root. Use this stated convention, not the alternative convention that “order” means maximum fan-out. question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.

Let I be the number of internal nodes and let k_v be the number of key entries in internal node v. That node has k_v+1 children, so summing all internal-node child counts counts every tree edge exactly once:

Σ_internal v (k_v+1) = number of edges.

The whole tree has I+ℓ nodes and is connected and acyclic, so it has I+ℓ−1 edges. Therefore

Σ k_v + I = I+ℓ−1,
and hence Σ k_v = ℓ−1.

This argument includes the root, whose minimum occupancy differs from other internal nodes. It does not depend on the height, branching distribution, or order d, only on the fact that every internal node has one more child than key entries.

For a root with three leaf children, there are two root keys and ℓ−1=2. If an internal node with five leaf children is inserted one level lower, its four keys and the necessary separator keys above it still obey the same identity. The result counts stored separator entries in internal nodes; it is not the number of data records in the leaves, nor a claim about the number of distinct values across the entire B+-tree. Leaf keys can have different occupancy conventions without affecting this edge-count identity.

All leaves are at equal edge-distance h from the root. Use this stated convention, not the alternative convention that “order” means maximum fan-out. For d=4 and exactly 52 leaves, find the maximum number of internal nodes.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
With 52 leaves, the total number of internal key entries is 52−1=51. If there are I internal nodes, the root uses at least one key and every other internal node uses at least d=4. Hence

1+4(I−1)≤51,
so 4I≤54 and I≤13.

An upper bound alone is not enough: equal leaf depth might prevent attaining it. Here it is attainable. Build a height-3 tree as follows:
Depth 0: one root with two children (one key).
Depth 1: two internal nodes, each with five children (four keys each).
Depth 2: ten internal nodes. Give eight of them five leaf children and two of them six leaf children.
Depth 3: 8·5+2·6=52 leaves.

Every nonroot internal node has five or six children, within the permitted five-to-nine range for d=4. All leaves are at depth three. The internal-node count is 1+2+10=13, and their key total is 1+8+8·4+2·5=51, confirming the arithmetic.

Thus 13 is both an upper bound and an achievable maximum. Treating order 4 as a maximum of four children would use a different B+-tree definition and give a wrong result for the convention explicitly supplied in this paper.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_text: In this question a B+-tree of order d has d to 2d key entries in each nonroot internal node, and an internal node with M keys has M+1 children. An internal root has 1 to 2d keys. All leaves are at equal edge-distance h from the root. Use this stated convention, not the alternative convention that “order” means maximum fan-out. For h≥1, find the minimum number of leaves.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
Since h≥1, the root is internal. Its minimum one key gives a minimum of two children. Every other internal node has at least d keys, hence at least d+1 children.

At depth 1 there are therefore at least 2 nodes. At depth 2 there are at least 2(d+1), and continuing to the leaf level h gives

minimum leaves = 2(d+1)^(h−1).

The exponent is h−1 because the first branching step is performed by the root, with minimum fan-out two; the remaining h−1 steps have minimum fan-out d+1. Multiplying by d rather than d+1 would confuse the minimum number of keys with the number of child pointers.

The bound is attainable: give the root exactly two children and every other internal node exactly d+1 children, stopping with leaves at depth h. All nonroot internal nodes then have exactly d keys, the root has exactly one, and every leaf lies at the required common depth. For h=1 the tree is a root with two leaf children, and the formula gives 2. For d=4,h=3 it gives 2·5²=50 leaves, consistent with the 52-leaf construction in the companion part. A tree of height zero is outside this subpart and would instead consist of a single leaf.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_title: Minimum DFA for two divisibility conditions
question_text: Construct a finite-state machine with the minimum number of states accepting exactly the strings over {a,b} whose number of a symbols is divisible by 2 and number of b symbols is divisible by 3.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
The future acceptance of a prefix depends on two remainders, not on the order of its symbols. Let qij mean that the prefix contains i a's modulo 2 and j b's modulo 3. Use Q={q00,q01,q02,q10,q11,q12}; start at q00 and make only q00 accepting. An a toggles i, while a b advances j modulo 3.

State    on a    on b    Accepting?
q00      q10     q01     yes
q01      q11     q02     no
q02      q12     q00     no
q10      q00     q11     no
q11      q01     q12     no
q12      q02     q10     no

This table completely specifies the machine and can be drawn as two three-state b-cycles with paired a-transitions between them. By induction on input length, its state is always the pair of remainders claimed above. Therefore it accepts exactly the required strings, including the empty string because zero is divisible by both divisors.

To prove minimum size, first note that every qij is reachable by a^i b^j. Next take any distinct qij and qkl. Append the suffix a^((-i) mod 2)b^((-j) mod 3). From qij this reaches q00 and accepts. From qkl it reaches the nonzero remainder pair ((k−i) mod 2,(l−j) mod 3), so it rejects. Every pair of states is thus distinguishable by a common suffix. The six distinct residual languages require at least six DFA states; our six-state construction meets this lower bound. Merely multiplying 2 by 3 would suggest the answer but would not, without distinguishability, prove minimality.
derived_answer: Six-state DFA tracking (#a mod 2, #b mod 3); start and only accepting state q00.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: A language L is accepted by a finite-state machine. Prove that finite-state machines also accept L′={s: ss′∈L for some string s′} and Lᴿ={s: s is the reversal of some string in L}.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
Begin with a DFA M=(Q,Σ,δ,q0,F) for L. This loses no generality because any finite-state recognizer can be determinized. The two constructions solve different problems: L′ consists of prefixes that can still be completed to an accepted word; Lᴿ reverses complete accepted words.

Prefix construction: compute C={q∈Q: δ*(q,t)∈F for some t∈Σ*}. These are exactly the states from which some accepting state is reachable, found by a reverse graph search starting at F. Keep Q,Σ,δ,q0 unchanged and replace the accepting set F by C. The new machine accepts s precisely when δ*(q0,s) belongs to C, which is equivalent to the existence of t with δ*(q0,st)∈F. That is exactly s∈L′. No new states are needed. If L is nonempty, q0∈C and ε is a prefix; if L is empty, C is empty and no word is accepted.

Reversal construction: retain all old states and reverse every labeled transition. For each δ(p,a)=q, add an a-transition q→p. Introduce a fresh start state r with ε-transitions to every f∈F, and make q0 the sole final state. The result is generally nondeterministic because reversing edges can create several transitions with the same label. A path q0 --a1...an--> f in the old machine becomes f --an...a1--> q0 in the new one, and the converse follows by reversing the path again. Thus exactly the reversed words are accepted. If a DFA is required, apply ε-closure and subset construction. Simply exchanging start/final states without reversing edges, or reversing edges while insisting on a single old final as start, would not establish closure for arbitrary L.
derived_answer: For prefixes, accept all states that can reach an old final state. For reversal, reverse edges and exchange starts/finals using an ε-NFA.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_title: Unambiguous grammar for a Pascal subset
question_text: A language L is a subset of Pascal with expressions using only + and <, assignment statements, while statements, and compound statements begin ... end. Give an unambiguous grammar. The source does not specify lexical details, empty statements, or a trailing-semicolon convention.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
Here is one unambiguous grammar under the conventional choices that + binds more tightly than <, + associates to the left, and < is nonassociative. The lexer supplies tokens id and num; reserved words are distinct tokens, and := is assignment. Start symbol S denotes one statement.

S → id := E | while E do S | begin L end
L → S R
R → ; S R | ε
E → A | A < A
A → A + P | P
P → id | num | ( E )

The grammar deliberately uses nonempty compound statements with semicolons between statements, not after the last one. If empty blocks are required, add the separate production S→begin end. If an optional trailing semicolon is required, replace R by R→ε | ; T and T→ε | S R. These are explicit syntax extensions, not facts supplied by the question.

The expression hierarchy enforces a unique outer operator structure. An unparenthesized < must be the single comparison at the E level, so a+b<c+d parses as (a+b)<(c+d), and a<b<c is rejected unless parentheses explicitly group a comparison. Left recursion at A gives (a+b)+c, not a+(b+c). Parentheses delimit a complete nested expression. At statement level, id, while and begin select disjoint alternatives. The keyword do separates a while condition from its body; matching begin/end delimit a compound body, and semicolons separate its statements. There is no if/else construct and hence no dangling-else ambiguity.

For example, while x<y+1 do begin x:=x+1; y:=y+2 end has a unique parse: its loop body is the entire block, containing two assignments. Static type rules, such as requiring a Boolean while condition and compatible assignment types, belong to semantic analysis rather than this context-free grammar. The source does not uniquely determine every optional Pascal syntax feature; the stated conventions make this proposed grammar precise.
derived_answer: Use separate addition/comparison levels, one comparison per expression, and explicit statement/block productions.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text: The grammar is assign-stmt→LHS := E; E→E+T | T; T→T*V | V; V→id | (E); LHS→id. Variables have integer or real types. Convert expressions and assignments to postfix using typed tokens (+,i), (+,r), (*,i), (*,r), (:=,i), (:=,r). give-type(id) and give-name(id) return an identifier's type and name. Give a syntax-directed translation scheme. Mixed-type conversion and narrowing policies are not stated in the source.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
Use synthesized attributes X.type and X.code for E,T,V; use LHS.type and LHS.name for the assignment target. A code value is a token list, and || denotes concatenation. Identifier type is i or r. The following semantic actions specify the traversal without depending on a particular parser implementation.

V→id:       V.type=give-type(id); V.code=[give-name(id)]
V→(E):      V.type=E.type; V.code=E.code
T→V:        T.type=V.type; T.code=V.code
E→T:        E.type=T.type; E.code=T.code
LHS→id:     LHS.type=give-type(id); LHS.name=give-name(id)

For E→E1+T, let t=join(E1.type,T.type), where join(i,i)=i and every other numeric pair gives r. Set E.type=t and E.code=E1.code || T.code || [(+,t)]. For T→T1*V, set t=join(T1.type,V.type), T.type=t and T.code=T1.code || V.code || [(*,t)]. Subscripting E1 and T1 distinguishes the right-hand-side occurrence from the left-hand-side occurrence of the same nonterminal.

For assign-stmt→LHS:=E, check that the expression can be assigned to the destination. Emit [address(LHS.name)] || E.code || [(:=,LHS.type)]. Writing the LHS first follows the conventional postfix assignment form x y (:=,i); the assignment operator consumes the target address and the computed value. In a textual postfix language the name in that first position can denote its address implicitly.

A necessary semantic convention: with precisely the six listed typed operator tokens, the r arithmetic operators must accept integer operands by implicit widening, and (:=,r) must widen an integer value when needed. Under that convention the rules above handle mixed expressions. For integer x,y and real z, the translation of z:=x+y*z is z x y z (*,r) (+,r) (:=,r). Multiplication is emitted first, preserving the grammar's precedence. A real-to-integer assignment is rejected unless an explicit narrowing rule has been authorized.

If the target instead requires both operands already to have the operator's physical type, implicit widening is unavailable. Then replace operand code c by c||[i2r] whenever its integer result is consumed as real, and similarly before assignment to a real target. This alternative introduces an extra conversion token not supplied in the question. Homogeneous expressions need no such extension. Type tags alone do not define a real-to-integer rounding rule or a machine-level cast. Keeping these conventions explicit avoids silently inventing conversion behavior while still giving a complete translation scheme for the stated operator alphabet.
derived_answer: Synthesize type and postfix code; choose numeric promotion for each operator, emit left operand then right operand then typed operator, and check assignment compatibility.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_title: Five activation records with nested recursion
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
Distinguish a procedure's lexical parent from the activation that calls it. The dynamic link records the caller; the static link records the active instance of the enclosing lexical scope. Calls to A from inside B are recursive calls to a procedure declared directly inside Main, not declarations of a new A inside B.

Trace the shown calls. Main calls A1, which calls B1. B1's call to C1 creates only the fourth record, and C1 makes no further calls. C1 returns before the following call to A2, so its record has been removed. A2 is then the fourth record, and its call to B2 creates the fifth. At any matching five-record stage of this call pattern, the active chain is therefore:

Stack position   Activation   Local slot   Dynamic link   Static link
TOP              B2           B2.Z         A2             A2
                 A2           A2.Y         B1             Main
                 B1           B1.Z         A1             A1
                 A1           A1.Y         Main           Main
BOTTOM           Main         Main.X       null           null

Other ordinary record fields, such as a return address and saved registers, may exist but are not assigned values by the problem. A1.Y and A2.Y are distinct storage cells, as are B1.Z and B2.Z. No numeric values for X,Y,Z can be recovered from the ellipses. The completed C1 record, including its separate C1.Z slot, is absent.

The dynamic chain is B2→A2→B1→A1→Main. The different static chain from B2 is B2→A2→Main. In particular, A2's static link must not point to B1 merely because B1 called it. To create A2, B1 can follow its own static chain B1→A1→Main to find A's lexical parent. This is the central distinction the example tests. GateForum's available copy ends in the middle of this program; the complete call structure and five-record question are available only in the GFG reproduction.
derived_answer: Bottom to top: Main, A1, B1, A2, B2. Dynamic links follow the call chain; static links B2→A2, A2→Main, B1→A1, A1→Main.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_title: Equivalence partition of a Mealy machine
question_text:
The Mealy state table gives (next state,output) for inputs 0 and 1:
A: 0→(B,1), 1→(H,1)
B: 0→(F,1), 1→(D,1)
C: 0→(D,0), 1→(E,1)
D: 0→(C,0), 1→(F,1)
E: 0→(D,1), 1→(C,1)
F: 0→(C,1), 1→(C,1)
G: 0→(C,1), 1→(D,1)
H: 0→(C,0), 1→(A,1).
No initial state is specified. Find the equivalence partition of its states.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
Two Mealy states are equivalent if every finite input string produces the same output string from either state. In particular they must first agree on their immediate output for each input. The output pairs are (1,1) for A,B,E,F,G and (0,1) for C,D,H. This gives the initial partition P0={ABEFG,CDH}.

Refine each block according to the blocks reached on inputs 0 and 1, while retaining the output test. In P0, A and B lead respectively to blocks (ABEFG,CDH); E,F,G lead to (CDH,CDH); and C,D,H lead to (CDH,ABEFG). Hence P1={AB,EFG,CDH}.

Now use P1 to distinguish formerly similar successor states. A reaches (AB,CDH), whereas B reaches (EFG,CDH), splitting A from B. C and D both reach (CDH,EFG), whereas H reaches (CDH,AB), splitting H from CD. The states E,F,G still both transition into CDH. Thus P2={A,B,CD,EFG,H}.

Check stability: C and D have equal outputs and both go into CD on 0 and EFG on 1. Each of E,F,G has output 1 on both inputs and goes into CD on both inputs. No further split is needed. The singleton blocks trivially satisfy stability, so P2 is the equivalence partition.

Refinement never separates equivalent states: a split witnesses a finite input on which outputs eventually differ. For example, A and B are distinguished by 000, producing 111 and 110 respectively; H and C are distinguished by 100, producing 111 and 110. Conversely, a stable equal-output partition guarantees equal output sequences by induction on input length. This proves both directions, rather than guessing equivalent states from one-step transitions alone.

question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
The equivalence blocks are {A},{B},{C,D},{E,F,G},{H}. Replace every original destination by its block name, keeping the original output. The reduced table is:

Present state   input 0: next/output   input 1: next/output
A               B/1                    H/1
B               EFG/1                  CD/1
CD              CD/0                   EFG/1
EFG             CD/1                   CD/1
H               CD/0                   A/1

For example, C goes to D/0 and E/1, whereas D goes to C/0 and F/1. Once C,D are both named CD and E,F,G are all named EFG, those two rows become identical. Similarly, E,F,G all reduce to the row CD/1, CD/1. Therefore the choice of a representative inside a merged block does not affect the quotient table.

Why is this minimal rather than merely smaller? Output-based refinement begins with {ABEFG,CDH}, refines to {AB,EFG,CDH}, and then to the five displayed blocks, which are stable. Distinct resulting blocks have some finite distinguishing input, so no further merger preserves all output behavior. Five states are necessary to represent the behavior of all states in the given table.

No start state is printed, so the table does not justify inventing one or removing states as unreachable from it. This is minimization of the supplied machine's state behaviors. If a separate initial-state specification were supplied, one would additionally check reachability before reporting the size of a recognizer from that particular start. The table remains a Mealy table: outputs label transitions, not states, and a Moore-machine reinterpretation would be a different problem.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_title: Minimal SOP of a five-factor function
question_text: f=(¬w+y)(¬x+y)(w+¬x+z)(¬w+z)(¬x+z), where + is Boolean OR, juxtaposition is AND, and ¬ is complement. Express f in minimal sum-of-products form. The source requests only the answer; the derivation is included for learning.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
Group the two factors sharing ¬w and the two sharing ¬x. The Boolean identity (a+b)(a+c)=a+bc gives
(¬w+y)(¬w+z)=¬w+yz,
(¬x+y)(¬x+z)=¬x+yz.
Applying the same identity with the common term yz gives (¬w+yz)(¬x+yz)=¬w¬x+yz. The original function is therefore (¬w¬x+yz)(w+¬x+z).

The remaining factor is redundant. Whenever ¬w¬x=1, its term ¬x makes w+¬x+z true. Whenever yz=1, its term z makes that factor true. Thus multiplying by it changes neither product term and f=¬w¬x+yz.

To justify minimality, not just equivalence, consider the true input 0000 in variable order wxyz. Any implicant covering it must require w=0 and x=0: changing w alone gives 1000, which is false, and changing x alone gives 0100, which is false. Its largest covering cube is therefore ¬w¬x. At 1111, changing y alone or z alone makes f false, so an implicant covering that point must require y=z=1. Its largest covering cube is yz. A single product cannot cover both 0000 and 1111 without allowing false inputs, since they disagree on every variable. Hence at least two terms and at least four literals are needed. The expression above uses exactly two two-literal terms and is minimal.

As a separate finite check, its 1-minterms are 0,1,2,3,7,11,15. Evaluating all 16 assignments agrees with the visually read five-factor source formula. The complemented literals are essential: dropping a bar during OCR would change both the simplification and the following fault-count answer.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text: f=(¬w+y)(¬x+y)(w+¬x+z)(¬w+z)(¬x+z), where + is Boolean OR, juxtaposition is AND, and ¬ is complement. If the output line is stuck at 0, for how many input combinations is the output incorrect?
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
A stuck-at-zero output differs from the correct circuit exactly on inputs for which f should be 1. Inputs where f=0 still produce the correct visible output even though the circuit is faulty. First simplify the function to f=¬w¬x+yz using Boolean algebra.

Count the satisfying assignments by inclusion-exclusion. The term ¬w¬x fixes w=x=0 and leaves y,z free, giving four inputs. The term yz fixes y=z=1 and leaves w,x free, also giving four inputs. Their intersection fixes w=x=0,y=z=1, so that single input was counted twice. The number of distinct true inputs is 4+4−1=7.

In wxyz binary order, the erroneous inputs are 0000,0001,0010,0011,0111,1011,1111, corresponding to minterms 0,1,2,3,7,11,15. On each, the healthy output is 1 and the faulty output is 0. The other nine combinations have healthy output 0 and therefore do not expose this fault.

This count concerns one stuck-at fault on the final output line. It is not the count of faulty internal signals, nor a probability unless an input distribution is supplied. question_text: Three processes use a shared resource R mutually exclusively and nonpreemptively. Each has a unique fixed priority in {1,2,3}, with 3 highest. Shared state: semaphore mutex=1; semaphores proceed[1..3]=0; Boolean R_requested[1..3]=false; Boolean busy=false. Each process repeats request_R(my_priority); P(proceed[my_priority]); use R; release_R(my_priority). The supplied request_R(p) performs P(mutex); if busy then R_requested[p]:=true else begin V(proceed[p]); busy:=true end; V(mutex). Give release_R so each allocation goes to the highest-priority current requester. The shared-data declaration is printed as process[3] in the reproduction, while uses consistently say proceed; normalize that apparent naming typo explicitly.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
The release operation must inspect request flags and either transfer ownership or mark the resource free as one atomic critical section. Otherwise a new requester could take R between checking the flags and waking a waiting process. This code uses the same proceed array as the process and request routines; the source's isolated process spelling is treated as a declaration typo.

procedure release_R(my_priority):
    P(mutex)
    chosen := 0
    for p := 3 downto 1 do
        if R_requested[p] then
            chosen := p
            break
    if chosen = 0 then
        busy := false
    else
        R_requested[chosen] := false
        busy := true
        V(proceed[chosen])
    V(mutex)

The parameter my_priority identifies the releasing owner but is not needed to select the next one. Preconditions are that only the current owner calls release_R, each process has at most one outstanding request, and P/V have standard semaphore semantics. The no-waiter branch does not signal a semaphore: the next arriving requester will signal its own proceed entry in request_R before doing P on it.

Why keep busy true during handoff? A signaled process may not run immediately. The resource is nevertheless reserved for it; setting busy false would let a newcomer receive a second grant. Clearing the chosen flag prevents a later release from treating the same already-granted request as still waiting. Lower-priority flags remain set, preserving their requests.

Since priorities are unique and the loop scans 3,2,1, it chooses the highest pending priority at the moment of allocation. A higher-priority process arriving after that atomic choice must wait: the resource is nonpreemptive, so priority does not revoke an existing grant. At most one grant exists at a time, maintaining mutual exclusion. This scheme can starve a low-priority requester if higher-priority requests keep arriving; starvation freedom was not requested and does not follow from strict priority allocation.
derived_answer: Under mutex, select the highest set request flag, clear it and signal that process while retaining busy=true; set busy=false only if no process waits.
