question_title: Right-linear grammar counts a modulo three
question_text_status: source reference only; consult reproduction wording/options and source_issue_note
solution: Interpret S,A,B as states tracking the number of a symbols modulo3: a advances S→A→B→S, while b leaves the state unchanged. Terminating production S→b ends with residue0, and B→a also ends with residue0. Consequently every generated word has #a divisible by3. Conversely any nonempty word with that property can be scanned along these transitions; if its last symbol is b it terminates via S→b, and if its last symbol is a it terminates via B→a. Thus L={w in {a,b}^+ : #a(w)≡0 mod3}, option C in the stated positive-word universe.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text_status: source reference only; consult reproduction wording/options and source_issue_note
solution: Under repetition-free enumeration, both S1 and S2 hold (A). For S1, first decide membership of both components in recursive L1; if either is absent reject, otherwise run A until both appear and compare their unique indices. For S2, if L1 is empty it is recursive. Otherwise fix its first enumerated word w1. Decide whether x is in L1 by accepting x=w1 and otherwise asking the L2 decider whether w1#x belongs. Every other word appears later, so this is correct. The S2 argument also survives repetitions. However, if arbitrary repetitions are permitted, S1 can fail: let recursive L1 consist of all distinct tags a_e and b_e. Enumerate each b_e before its a_e, and repeat b_e after a_e exactly if machine e halts, using dovetailing. Then a_e#b_e belongs to L2 exactly for halting machines, making L2 nonrecursive despite recursive L1. Thus with repetitions allowed only S2 is necessarily true (C). No unconditional option is assigned without fixing the enumeration convention.

question_title: Unique light edge of a cut

solution: Let T be a minimum spanning tree. If its edges omit the unique lightest crossing edge e, insert e into T, making a cycle. That cycle contains another edge f crossing the same cut. Connectivity is implicitly required for a spanning tree (otherwise use a minimum spanning forest in relevant components). GFG prints this answer beside B after a blank A; GateForum prints it as A. question_title: Cycles through an undirected DFS leaf
question_text_status: source reference only; consult reproduction wording/options
solution: In an undirected DFS, every non-tree edge joins a vertex to an ancestor. Since u is a DFS leaf, all its neighbors lie on its single root-to-u tree path. Let w be its highest ancestor-neighbor. The tree path w to u plus the edge uw forms a cycle containing every neighbor of u, since all those neighbors lie between w and u. Degree at least two ensures a genuine cycle. Thus D. Two distinct cycles sharing only a root refute the asserted common cycle; other DFS graphs refute the universal common neighbor and separator assertions.

question_title: Push and pop counts for a two-stack queue
question_text_status: source reference only; consult reproduction wording/options
solution: Let t be the number of items moved from S1 to S2 and d the number of successful deletes. Then x=n+t pushes and y=t+d pops, with d≤t≤n. If all m deletes succeed, d=m, so n+m≤x≤2n and 2m≤y≤n+m. These are the tight intended bounds. The supplied reproduction prints x<2n in all four options, which fails when all n inserts precede a delete: t=n and x=2n. Furthermore arbitrary ordering permits deletes on an empty queue; then d need not equal m and the printed lower bounds can fail. If < were repaired to ≤ and successful deletions assumed, A states the tight bounds, but other looser options would also be true. Do not treat this reproduction as a sound unique-answer MCQ without checking a better source. The cleaner GateForum reproduction also prints x<2n in every option. Thus the strict-upper-bound defect persists across both third-party versions. A minimal counterexample is one insert followed by one delete: n=m=1 and x=y=2. solution: Only p and q can initially finish without another allocation. After both finish, available resources equal W=x_p+x_q. solution: In C, every string wxw^R has the same first and last symbol and length at least3. subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: Single-source shortest paths in an unweighted graph
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: BFS starts at S and discovers vertices in increasing number of edges from S. When a vertex is first discovered, its level is its shortest-path distance; parent pointers recover paths. With adjacency lists, every vertex and edge is processed O(1) times, giving O(V+E). DFS does not generally find shortest paths; generic Dijkstra adds priority-queue overhead, and Warshall solves a more expensive all-pairs/reachability problem. Thus D is the appropriate algorithm.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: Worst-case recursion depth of Euclid algorithm
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: For positive integers n≥m>0, Euclid replaces (n,m) by (m,n mod m). Within two recursive steps the larger argument decreases by at least a factor of two, so there are O(log n) recursive calls. Consecutive Fibonacci inputs attain a matching lower bound: their quotients are one for most steps, and F_k grows exponentially in k, giving Θ(log n) calls in the worst case (A). The statement does not say worst case: when m divides n, there are zero recursive calls. Therefore Θ(log n) is not a pointwise bound for every input satisfying n≥m. Positive m is also necessary to avoid remainder by zero.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_title: Satisfying at least half the clauses of a CNF formula
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: For the conventional setting in which each clause contains at least one literal, consider any assignment and its bitwise complement. Every clause is satisfied by at least one of the two: choose any literal in it, which is true in one assignment. Hence the two assignments together satisfy at least m clause occurrences, and one satisfies at least m/2. This proves A. B fails for (x)∧(¬x), and the same half-clause guarantee rules out C. If empty clauses are permitted, the unstated nonempty-clause assumption matters: a formula consisting only of empty clauses is never satisfied at all, so A would fail and C could hold. The intended CNF convention excludes this degenerate case.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: A globally minimum-weight edge and minimum spanning trees
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: Take any MST T. If e is absent, adding it creates a cycle. Every edge of that cycle has weight at least w by global minimality of w, and none can have weight greater than w: exchanging such an edge for e would make a strictly cheaper spanning tree. Thus all cycle edges have weight w, proving B; exchanging any one of them for e produces an MST containing e, proving A. Every MST contains an edge of weight w by the same argument (or contains e itself), proving C. However a triangle with all edges weight w has MSTs omitting any chosen edge, so e need not belong to every MST. D is false, assuming the usual loop-free graph convention.

question_title: Regular grammars versus existence of LR(1) grammars
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: P is false: the right-linear regular grammar S→aA | aB, A→b, B→c has two alternatives whose FIRST sets both contain a, so this particular grammar is not LL(1). Determinism gives at most one alternative per terminal; epsilon is selected at end of input. This yields an LL(1), hence LR(1), grammar for the regular language (or use the standard inclusion of regular languages in deterministic context-free languages). Thus P false and Q true, option C.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_title: Register allocation and MOV count in a basic block
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: For expression-preserving code generation, three MOVs suffice: MOV a,R1; ADD b,R1; MOV c,R2; ADD d,R2; SUB e,R2; SUB R1,R2; MOV R2,t4. The specified source-minus-destination semantics gives R1=t1, R2=t2 then t3=e−t2 then t4=t1−t3. There are two loads to initialize the two independently computed subexpressions and one store, yielding the intended option B (3). This minimum presumes the usual task of generating code for the given expression structure. If algebraic reassociation is allowed, two MOVs suffice: MOV c,R1; ADD d,R1; SUB e,R1; SUB a,R1; ADD b,R1; MOV R1,t4. This computes t4=a−(e−(c+d))+b. Furthermore, if arbitrary arithmetic instructions may initialize a register, SUB R1,R1 makes zero; replacing the initial MOV c,R1 by SUB R1,R1; ADD c,R1 leaves only the final MOV. Hence the literal unrestricted minimum is not 3, and the scope assumption must be disclosed; B is an intended, conditional answer rather than an unconditional theorem.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_title: Two intent flags give mutual exclusion but may deadlock
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: Under the standard sequentially consistent, atomic-read/write pseudocode model, each process sets its own wants flag before testing the other's flag and keeps it true throughout its critical section. Thus both cannot pass their tests and overlap in the critical section: whichever passes first prevents the other entering until it clears its flag. However, if both set their flags before either tests the other, each spins forever, giving deadlock. Thus D describes the decisive combination: mutual exclusion holds but deadlock prevention fails. Strict alternation is not required; one process can repeatedly enter while the other does not request entry. Option B needs care: under a broad interpretation that bounded waiting guarantees eventual entry, deadlock also violates it. In the usual bounded-overtaking formulation, distinguish this progress failure from another process overtaking a waiter indefinitely; the latter cannot occur here. D is the intended most specific answer, while the phrasing of B can be read more broadly.

question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: Under standard textbook normalization conventions, a two-attribute relation is BCNF: a nontrivial dependency from one attribute to the other makes its determinant a key. Single-attribute candidate keys have no proper nonempty subset, so no partial dependency prevents 2NF. In 3NF a non-key determinant may determine a prime attribute, permitting the transitive dependency in C. BCNF instead requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey, so it excludes a transitive dependency through a non-key determinant. D is the intended false statement. Here transitive dependency means the normalization violation through a non-superkey, not merely any composable implication. The claims about two-attribute relations and singleton keys also assume the textbook convention excluding nontrivial empty-determinant dependencies. If such dependencies are allowed, R(A,B) with ∅ -> B and candidate key A violates both BCNF and 2NF: ∅ is not a superkey, and the nonprime B depends on a proper subset of key A. Consequently A and B are also false under that fully general interpretation, so D is the intended answer only with this convention.

question_title: Majority test in a sorted array
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: If a value occurs more than n/2 times, it must occupy the middle array position. Take that value as candidate and use binary searches for its first and last occurrences; accept exactly when the count exceeds n/2. This needs Θ(log n) comparisons in the worst case. A logarithmic lower bound follows by locating a candidate-block boundary among linearly many possible positions while distinguishing length floor(n/2) from floor(n/2)+1. Sortedness is essential; without it a linear majority scan is needed. Thus B.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_title: Maximum splits in an order-four B-tree
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: An order-four B-tree has at most three keys per node. The maximum is five splits. For ordinary overflow-triggered insertion, inserting 1 through 10 in ascending order and promoting the lower middle key splits a leaf on insertions 4, 6, 8 and 10; the fourth leaf split also overflows and splits the root. For a timing-independent bound, after L leaf splits there are L+1 nonempty leaves. A B-tree with L+1 leaves has exactly L separator keys in all internal nodes combined: each internal node has one fewer key than children, and summing over the tree gives leaves minus one. Consequently n≥(L+1)+L=2L+1. With n=10, L≤4. Under overflow-triggered insertion, the first internal split needs the root to receive four separators from four leaf splits. With no further leaf split possible, no second internal split can occur. Thus there is at most one internal/root split and the total is at most 4+1=5. Under preemptive splitting, the full root may instead split after three leaf splits, distributing its three separators into a new root with one key and two internal children with one key each. At most one further leaf split is possible, which can increase only one such child to two keys; no internal node can become full again. The same upper bound therefore holds, and increasing-key insertion attains five splits under this convention too.

question_title: Two edge-disjoint spanning trees and connectivity
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: The claim about two internally vertex-disjoint paths is not guaranteed. Take two copies of K4 sharing exactly one vertex: n=7 and m=12=2n−2. Each K4 decomposes into two spanning trees (for example a path on its four vertices and its complementary path); joining corresponding trees at the shared vertex gives two edge-disjoint spanning trees of the whole graph. The common vertex is nevertheless an articulation vertex, so paths between the two sides must share it. A is true because each tree induces a forest with at most k−1 edges on a nonempty k-vertex set. B is true since each spanning tree contributes a distinct edge across every nontrivial cut. C follows by taking the unique path in each of the two edge-disjoint trees.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: Quicksort recurrence from bounded partition sizes
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: Each recursive subproblem has size at most 4n/5, because each side has at least n/5 elements. With the usual monotone worst-case upper-bound interpretation of T and linear partitioning cost, both recursive costs are bounded individually by T(4n/5), so T(n)≤2T(4n/5)+n, option C. This loose recurrence follows immediately from the given size bounds. The tempting expression T(n/5)+T(4n/5)+n assumes that the most unequal permitted split maximizes the sum of recursive costs; monotonicity alone does not establish that. More precisely the general recurrence is T(n)≤max_{n/5≤k≤4n/5}{T(k)+T(n−k)}+O(n), ignoring pivot/rounding constants. The standard comparison model includes linear partition/pivot overhead; the statement does not specify the cost of an arbitrary extra pivot-selection procedure.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: Dijkstra on the given negative-edge graph
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: All vertices receive the correct distance despite the negative edges. From a, settle b at 1, which sets c=3 and e=−2. Settle e at −2, then f at 0, setting g=3. Vertices c and g tie at 3. Whichever is handled first, c sets h=3−5=−2 before h is settled (if g was handled first it only proposes h=5). Vertex h proposes e=−1, not an improvement over −2. Vertex d gets 6 from c and offers no improvement to a or g. Final distances (a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h)=(0,1,3,6,−2,0,3,−2). They also satisfy every edge relaxation inequality, with each value attained by a path, proving optimality. Negative edges invalidate Dijkstra’s general guarantee, but do not force failure on every particular input.

question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: Θ(n) time is sufficient and necessary. Read the postorder sequence backward: the next element is the root, followed by the right subtree in reverse postorder and then the left. A recursive builder with allowed key interval (low,high) consumes a value only if it belongs in that interval; after creating a node with key r, build the right interval (r,high), then the left (low,r). Each key is consumed once and there are O(n) calls, so the time is O(n). Distinct BST keys and their ordering make the construction unique. Reading and outputting n nodes requires Ω(n), yielding Θ(n).

question_title: Batch insertion into a binary heap
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: Append all n new elements to the existing n-element heap array, then run bottom-up BUILD-HEAP on the resulting 2n elements. Its total sift-down work is O(n), since the number of nodes of height h decreases geometrically and Σh/2^h is constant. Reading/storing n new elements requires Ω(n), so the optimum total is Θ(n), option B. The permission to insert them in a batch is crucial: n separate ordinary heap insertions can require Θ(n log n).

question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options

Even a recursively enumerable set itself need not be recursive. A holds by the subset construction for NFAs. B holds because a deterministic Turing machine can dovetail the finitely branching computation tree of a nondeterministic machine, accepting exactly when an accepting branch is found. C holds because a finite automaton can be converted to a right-linear context-free grammar.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: Under the conventional grammar-transformation interpretation, I, III and IV are true, giving C. I refers to eliminating left recursion using right-recursive auxiliaries and the symmetric transformation for right recursion; it does not mean every context-free grammar becomes a right-linear regular grammar. II is false as stated: if ε belongs to the language, removing every ε-production cannot preserve that language, since no nonempty sentential form can derive the empty string without one. III is a right-linear grammar, possibly with multi-terminal labels; expanding labels into paths yields a finite automaton, so its language is regular. IV is true in the at-most-two-children sense of binary tree: CNF uses A→BC or A→a (and possibly the special start ε-rule), so no derivation-tree node has more than two children.

question_title: Matching language patterns to compiler requirements
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: The matching is E–R, F–P, G–Q, H–S, option C. E requires the same identifier string in declaration and use, modeled by the copy language wcw. F matches counts of formal and actual parameters; a^n b^m c^n d^m models the two cross-referenced counts. G is modeled by X→XbX | XcX | dXf | g: b and c act as binary operators, d/f as matched opening/closing parentheses, and g as an operand. H is modeled by X→bXb | cXc | ε, which generates even-length palindromes. These are structural analogies, not claims that the small grammars capture every feature of a programming language or all odd-length palindromes.

solution: Name the lower start state L, upper-left state A and upper-right state B. Every automaton accepts ε at L; every nonempty accepted path begins with 0 from L to A. In P, cycles from A back to A are 00 via L or 01*1 via B, and a finishing path to either accepting state is represented by 01*. Hence P matches expression 1: ε+0(01*1+00)*01*. In Q, the A-cycles are 00 or 10*1, with final 0 to L, giving expression 2. In R, the A-cycles are 10 or 10*1, with final 1 to L, giving expression 3. In S, the same cycles apply but B is also accepting, so a final 10* covers both possible accepting destinations, giving expression 4. Thus P–1,Q–2,R–3,S–4, option C.

solution: I and IV are regular, giving A. I has expression a*(bb)*: n and m are independent and only the parity of the b-count is restricted. IV has expression (a|b)*c(a|b)* because x and y need not be equal. II is {a^(2m)b^m}; applying the pumping lemma to a^(2p)b^p pumps only a symbols and destroys the required 2:1 relation. subject: 07-compiler-design
question_title: Activation records, recursion and escaping closures
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: Under the standard language-runtime assumptions, II and V are true, giving A. I is false: recursive calls can have arbitrarily many simultaneously live instances of local variables, so one statically allocated activation record per procedure is insufficient even without globals or nested procedures. II is true: multilevel static access links/displays serve access to lexically enclosing procedures; without lexical nesting no multilevel environment chain is needed. III is false because dynamic stack allocation supports ordinary recursion. IV is false because nested procedures and recursion alone can use stack activation records with static/dynamic links. V describes a returned nested function that can retain its defining environment after the creator returns: pure stack allocation cannot preserve that environment, so escaping environments need extended lifetime, normally heap allocation or copying.

solution: The equivalence is with canonical LR(1), option B. An LALR state merges LR(1) states having the same LR(0) core and unions lookaheads. Suppose a merged state has a reduction A→α on lookahead a and a shift on a. The reduction/lookahead pair came from some original LR(1) state. The shift item is in the shared LR(0) core, so it also occurred in that very original state. Thus the shift-reduce conflict already existed before merging. Conversely a conflict in an original LR(1) state survives the merge. Merging can introduce reduce-reduce conflicts, but cannot create a new shift-reduce conflict. SLR/LR(0) may report conflicts avoided by finer LR(1) lookaheads.

solution: The congestion window grows exponentially over successive round-trip times in slow start, option D. In the simplified textbook model each acknowledged segment increases the window by one MSS; a window of W segments produces about W acknowledgments in one RTT, so the window becomes approximately 2W. After k such rounds it is approximately 2^k times its initial value, until reaching a threshold or encountering loss. Growth is per ACK rather than continuous time; delayed ACKs and practical implementations affect the precise factor but not the intended exponential-versus-linear distinction.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_title: TCP connect before the server calls accept
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: The client connect() can return successfully, option A. After socket(), bind() and listen(), the server kernel has a listening TCP endpoint and can complete the three-way handshake while the server process is descheduled. The resulting established connection waits in the listener’s accept queue; accept() subsequently removes an entry and returns a connected socket to the server process. Hence user-space accept() is not required for the client handshake to complete. The intended setting assumes an available backlog slot and normal network operation; incidental loss, queue exhaustion or unrelated errors can of course affect real calls.

solution: The semaphore x_b protects the shared count and must start unlocked at 1. The semaphore y_b represents the waiting gate and must start at 0, so a P operation with negative count blocks. Thus the required initial values are (1,0), option C. This answers the initialization question, not a proof of the whole implementation. Under ordinary saturating binary-semaphore semantics the shown implementation can lose a wakeup: two P callers decrement to -2 and pause before P_b(y_b); two V callers then both signal y_b before either waiter consumes it, leaving only one stored signal. question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: Let S=2^32, clock rate C=1000/s, packet lifetime M=64 s, and a constant-rate connection start at time 0 with initial sequence number 0, so its sequence trajectory is q(t)=rt. For r<C, the next occurrence of this sequence value on the returning clock trajectory is at time (S+rt)/C. To let a packet sent at t expire before that clock reuse, require (S+rt)/C−t≥M, equivalently (C−r)t≤S−CM. Requiring this throughout a connection of duration D therefore gives r≥C−(S−CM)/D (with nonnegative rates understood). If the intended duration is one clock cycle, D=S/C, this becomes r≥C²M/S=1000²×64/2^32=0.0149011612/s, closest to A, 0.015/s. This is an exact conditional derivation under the stated constant-rate, returning-clock model. The question does not actually specify D: the tiny minimum is therefore conditional on the one-clock-cycle interpretation, not a universal minimum. In particular, every r<C eventually reaches the returning forbidden strip if the connection continues indefinitely. The original 1/M shortcut is unjustified and is not used. Conceptual reference: Tanenbaum, Computer Networks, 5th edition, Figure 6-10 (clock-based forbidden regions); https://csc-knu.github.io/sys-prog/books/Andrew%20S.%20Tanenbaum%20-%20Computer%20Networks.pdf .

question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: P0 consumes the initial S0 permit and prints once, then enables P1 and P2. Each of those processes releases S0 exactly once. If both releases occur before P0 next waits on S0, binary saturation coalesces them into one permit, allowing only one further print: total 2. If P0 consumes the first released permit before the other process releases S0, it receives two separate permits and prints three times total. Thus 2 or 3 prints are possible, so the only correct choice is A, at least twice. This assumes ordinary progress/eventual scheduling; an adversarial scheduler that permanently starves runnable processes defeats any eventual-print guarantee. A counting semaphore would instead give exactly three.

solution: For each vertex v_i with i≥3, its lightest incident edge is (v_(i−2), v_i), with weight 2i−2. The edge (v_1, v_2), of weight 3, is likewise the unique lightest edge incident to v_1 and to v_2. By the cut property all these edges must belong to an MST. They form two parity chains joined by (v_1, v_2), so they are connected and contain exactly n−1 edges, hence already form a spanning tree. Its weight is 3+sum from i=3 to n of (2i−2)=3+2[(n−1)n/2−1]=n²−n+1, option B.

question_title: Local minima on a closed interval
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: On the restricted domain [π/4, 7π/4], the left endpoint π/4 is a one-sided local minimum because sin x increases immediately to its right. The interior stationary points satisfy cos x=0: π/2 is a maximum and 3π/2 is a minimum. The right endpoint is not a minimum because sin x increases toward it from the left. Thus the restricted-domain convention yields two local minima, π/4 and 3π/2, D. If local extrema are defined to exclude endpoints, only the interior minimum remains; the official key uses the former convention.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: The overbars in statements 2–4 are essential: each asks about the complement of L. Regular languages are closed under complementation (complete a DFA and exchange accepting/nonaccepting states), and recursive languages are closed under complementation (swap the outcomes of a halting decider), so 3 and 4 always answer yes. Whether an arbitrary program ever outputs is undecidable by simulating a machine and printing only if it halts. For a context-free input language, deciding whether its complement is context-free is an undecidable grammar-property problem; lack of closure alone would not suffice to prove undecidability. Thus the intended decidable entries are 3 and 4, D. For a reduction justifying statement 2, fix a CFL H over a separate alphabet Γ whose complement is the non-CFL {a^k b^k c^k: k≥0}; H is context-free by expressing unequal counts and malformed strings as a union of CFLs. Given a CFG language L over Σ, construct the CFL K consisting of L#Γ*, Σ*#H, and all malformed strings outside Σ*#Γ*. Its complement is (Σ*−L)#(Γ*−H). If L=Σ*, this is empty and context-free. Otherwise, choosing w∉L and intersecting with regular w#Γ* leaves w#(Γ*−H), which is not context-free (remove the fixed prefix by left quotient). Therefore a test for context-freeness of complements would decide the undecidable CFG-universality problem.

question_title: Squaring edge weights and minimum spanning trees
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: Squaring positive weights preserves every pairwise edge order and equality. Consequently it preserves the set of minimum spanning trees: any chosen MST of G remains an MST of G′, although independently chosen T and T′ can differ if the MST is not unique. For a fixed spanning tree with edge weights w_i, its new weight is Σw_i², while t²=Σw_i²+2Σ_{i<j}w_iw_j. With at least two edges this gives t′<t²; with one edge there is equality. Thus B describes a consistent common choice of tree on at least three vertices, but the unqualified statement T′=T need not hold when multiple MSTs exist, and small graphs also matter. The official entry is Marks to All. These are independent qualifications, not a claimed official cancellation rationale.

question_title: Lost unlock in a fetch-and-add lock
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: Suppose one process holds the lock with L=1. A waiter executes Fetch_And_Add, obtains old value 1 and changes L to 2, so it must execute the loop body. Before that body executes, the owner releases the lock by storing L=0. The waiter then executes its pending L=1 assignment, restoring a nonzero value even though nobody holds the lock. Subsequent tests keep failing and there need be no owner left to release it. Thus B identifies a failure even without arithmetic overflow.

question_title: Conditional second roll of a die
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: If the first roll is 6, success occurs immediately with probability 1/6; first rolls 4 or 5 stop unsuccessfully. For first roll 1, the second must be 5 or 6 (two outcomes); for 2 it must be 4, 5, 6 (three); for 3 it must be 3, 4, 5, 6 (four). Each ordered two-roll result has probability 1/36. Total success probability is 1/6+(2+3+4)/36=15/36=5/12, B. One-roll and two-roll terminal outcomes are not equiprobable.

solution: Ordinary mergesort uses O(n log n) comparisons to sort n strings. A lexicographic comparison can inspect all n characters, so the standard upper bound is O(n² log n), option B. The bound is tight in the usual character-by-character implementation: strings can share a prefix of length n−O(log n) and have suitably ordered distinct suffixes, so a worst-case merge pattern performs Θ(n log n) comparisons each costing Θ(n). Treating entire strings as unit-cost keys, using LCP-aware comparison, or restricting how many distinct strings exist changes the analysis; those are extra models not specified. question_title: Packet pipeline across three equal links
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: A packet takes 1000/10⁶ s=1 ms to transmit on each link. Each link propagation delay is 100, 000/10⁸ s=1 ms. With store-and-forward routers and no extra processing/queueing delays, the first packet reaches D after 3×(1+1)=6 ms. Subsequent packets emerge from the equal-rate pipeline 1 ms apart, so the final packet arrives at 6+999=1005 ms, A. Equivalently, total elapsed completion time is (1000+3−1)×1+3×1 ms. Summing the service time separately over all packets is not the elapsed file-transfer time asked for.

solution: The official Code A key awards Marks to All; it does not supply a numerical answer or an official explanation. To expose the conventions needed, take transmissions as RTT-sized rounds: the initial windows are 2, 4, 8, 9, 10 MSS, so a timeout in round 5 sets a halved threshold of 5 MSS under the usual round model. If the post-timeout window resets to the stated slow-start value 2 and slow-start growth is capped at the threshold, rounds 6–10 end with windows 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 MSS (A). With a one-MSS timeout restart and the same threshold-capping convention, they end with 2, 4, 5, 6, 7 MSS (C). Literal doubling across the threshold gives still other round traces. ACK-level growth and whether the quoted window belongs to the beginning or end of a transmission also need a convention. These conditional examples explain why one should not present a uniquely established numerical result from this wording; they are not claimed as the exam authority’s reason for the award.

solution: In C, the consumer first signals S to indicate readiness, then waits on R; the producer waits on S before signaling R after its item has been computed. The consumer reads the item only after that R handshake. Since the next S is not issued until the preceding consumer iteration finishes, signals cannot outrun the corresponding item and collapse in a binary semaphore. A deadlocks immediately because both sides initially wait on zero semaphores. B lacks a readiness handshake, so multiple signals can collapse. In D, the producer can signal R for the next item before the consumer consumes the preceding R, again collapsing signals. Thus C provides the required synchronization.

question_title: Reference parameter and multiplication evaluation order
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: The parameter declaration int &x is C++ reference syntax, not valid C. Every recursive invocation aliases the same p through x, whereas c is a private by-value copy. The four non-base calls increment p successively to 6, 7, 8 and 9; the fifth call returns 1 without incrementing p. In return f(x, c) * x, multiplication does not require the left operand to be evaluated first. If each call reads its right-hand x before executing the recursive call, the stored factors are 6, 7, 8, 9 and the return value is 6×7×8×9=3024 (A). If each call executes the recursive call before reading its right-hand x, all four factors are the final p=9 and the result is 9^4=6561 (B). Mixed choices can give other values. Under C++ rules sequencing a function’s execution as a unit relative to otherwise unsequenced outside evaluations, this is an unspecified operand-order issue; the recursive function call must not be confused with an unsequenced x++ written directly beside a read of x. The source does not prescribe an evaluation convention or a language version, so no unique numerical option follows. The official Code A key explicitly awards Marks to All. This record is classified under compiler parameter-passing/evaluation semantics, not as a valid C program.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_title: Minimum register spills with code motion
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: One spill store suffices. With registers R1, R2, start with a in R1 and b in R2. Compute R2←R1+R2 (c), store c once in spill slot S, and compute R2←R2×R2 (x). Compare R2 with R1. On the true branch compute y as R1←R1×R1. On the false branch execute: load R2←S; R2←R2×R1 (d); R2←R2×R2 (d²); load R2←S; R2←R2+R1 (e); R2←R2×R2 (e²). The computations d=c*a and e=c+a have been sunk into the false branch, where they are used, and arranged just before their respective squarings. Their former values are unused on the true branch, and all variables are dead after the segment, so this code motion preserves the required values. It performs one spill store and two reloads on the false path; reloads are not additional spills to memory. For the lower bound, after forming c the independent live values a and c already occupy both registers. Before the branch can be decided, at least one of d=c*a, e=c+a or x=c*c must be computed. If d or e is first, its result is needed for its later square while both a and c remain necessary for the other operations. If x is first, x and a are needed for the test while c is still needed on the false path. Thus the first such result forces three simultaneously needed values in a no-spill schedule, regardless of permitted reordering. A live value must be saved. Since recomputation and dead-code elimination are not allowed, zero spills is impossible and the minimum is one, option B.

solution: There are 2^20/(16×64)=2^10 cache sets. A 64-byte cache block uses six offset bits, so the ten set-index bits are virtual-address bits 6 through 15. From the preceding linked question, the page size is 8 KiB and the page offset consists of bits 0 through 12. Only seven set-index bits (6 through 12) lie inside the page offset and are automatically identical for synonyms. The remaining three bits (13 through 15) can differ between virtual aliases of the same physical page. Distinguishing 2^3=8 page colours, and requiring aliases of a physical page to use the same colour, makes all index bits agree. Thus eight colours are necessary and sufficient, option C. Equivalently, colours=(cache size)/(associativity×page size)=1 MiB/(16×8 KiB)=8.

question_title: Candidate keys from the functional dependencies
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: D never occurs on any right-hand side, so every key must contain D. The dependencies A→B, B→F, F→E and E→A form a reachability cycle among A, B, E, F. Starting from any one of those four attributes derives the other three, C and H through B→CFH, and G through F→EG. Consequently A+, B+, E+, F+ each equal {A, B, C, E, F, G, H}, missing only D. Thus AD, BD, DE and DF are candidate keys, and each is minimal. For completeness, any set containing none of A, B, E, F can include only C, D, G, H; its closure can at most add G via CH→G and can never reach that four-attribute cycle. Therefore every key includes at least one of A, B, E, F, and a minimal key includes exactly one together with D. There are precisely four candidate keys, option B.

solution: Atomic fields give 1NF. The candidate keys are AD, BD, DE, DF, so the prime attributes are A, B, D, E, F and the non-prime attributes are C, G, H. subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text_status: source reference only; consult original wording/options
solution: Each XOR delay is 2.4microseconds and each AND/OR delay1.2. A full adder made from two half adders has P=A XOR B, sum=P XOR Cin and Cout=AB+P*Cin. Its worst input-to-output delay is 4.8. Multiplying this black-box delay by four gives the published19.2. However in a gate-aware ripple circuit all four P signals are computed in parallel. The first carry settles by 4.8, and each later carry needs only AND+OR=2.4 more, giving carry delays4.8, 7.2, 9.6, 12; the last sum also settles by 9.6+2.4=12. Thus19.2 is a conservative lumped-stage estimate, not the tight standard gate-level propagation bound under simultaneous operand arrival. A fixed zero initial carry or different arrival assumptions can further change sensitized timing. The intended timing model is not explicit.
derived_answer: Official19.2 uses lumped full-adder delays; gate-aware model gives12

solution: Let F(n) be the maximum number of loop iterations with n queued values and no relevant stack entries. Until a minimum queued value is pushed, each value originally preceding that minimum is pushed at most once and popped at most once: popped items return behind the minimum. Thus this phase costs at most2n−1 iterations. Once the minimum is pushed it never pops, leaving at most n−1 values to process above it. Hence F(n)≤2n−1+F(n−1), giving F(n)≤n². A strictly descending initial queue attains equality at each phase, because all preceding values are pushed and popped and return in descending order behind the minimum. Therefore F(16)=256.

question_text: Given pqr≠0, p^(−x)=1/q, q^(−y)=1/r, r^(−z)=1/p, find xyz. Choices: A −1; B 1/(pqr); C 1; D pqr.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

Under the usual positive nonunit-base interpretation, taking reciprocals gives p^x=q, q^y=r and r^z=p. Logs therefore give x ln p=ln q, y ln q=ln r, z ln r=ln p. Multiplication cancels only when these logarithms are nonzero. That condition is not implied by pqr≠0. For example, choosing all bases 1 and x=y=z=2 satisfies the written equations but yields product 8.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

For positive p, q, r different from 1, the equations give x=log q/log p, y=log r/log q, z=log p/log r. Multiplying cancels the logarithms and gives xyz=1, C. But the stated condition pqr≠0 allows p=q=r=1; then all three equations hold for arbitrary x, y, z, so the product is undetermined. The official answer needs a nonunit-base/domain qualification.

Use triangle angle sums together with supplementary angles on straight lines. Label α=∠BAD, β=∠DEC, γ=∠BFC. Because AD and AE are the same ray and EC and EB are the same ray, triangle AEB has angles α and β at A and E. At B, extending AB to BF changes its interior angle to its supplement. subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text: A fair six-faced die has four green and two red faces. After seven independent rolls, which count is most likely? A 3 green/4 red; B 4/3; C 5/2; D 6/1.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

The event specifies a count, not a particular ordering. Therefore include the binomial factor: P(K=k)=C(7,k)(2/3)^k(1/3)^(7−k). For the four options, the numerators over the common denominator 3^7 are 280, 560, 672 and 448. Five greens has the largest numerator. Simply maximizing the probability of an individual ordered sequence would incorrectly ignore how many arrangements produce each count.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

If K counts green faces, K is binomial with n=7, p=2/3. Its unique mode is floor((7+1)·2/3)=5. Equivalently consecutive probability ratios are P(K=k+1)/P(K=k)=2(7−k)/(k+1), above1 through k=4 and below1 at k=5. Five green and two red is most likely, C.

question_text: C declares struct Ournode { char x,y,z; }; initializes p={'1','0','a'+2}; sets q=&p; and prints printf("%c, %c", *((char*)q+1), *((char*)q+2)). Choices: A 0, c; B 0, a+2; C '0', 'a+2'; D '0', 'c'.

solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

The cast occurs before pointer arithmetic: a char pointer advances by one byte, whereas adding 1 to a struct pointer would advance by a whole struct. Under the intended layout, offsets 1 and 2 select y and z. The expression 'a'+2 is evaluated numerically during initialization, not printed as source text. The %c conversion prints the represented character without surrounding quote marks. Keep the implementation assumptions below separate from the intended exam output.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

With consecutive char members at byte offsets0, 1, 2, the two dereferences read y and z. In an ASCII-compatible execution character set, y is the character0 and z is c from a+2, giving0, c, A. Strict ISO C permits internal struct padding and does not universally require contiguous alphabetic codes. The result therefore assumes the conventional padding-free char layout and character encoding used by the question.

question_text: A noncircular singly linked queue stores head and tail pointers. Enqueue inserts at head; dequeue removes tail. For n nodes, choose the optimal worst-case time pair: A Θ(1),Θ(1); B Θ(1),Θ(n); C Θ(n),Θ(1); D Θ(n),Θ(n).
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

Enqueue sets new.next=head and head=new, also initializing tail if previously empty. Tail removal must change the predecessor’s next pointer to null and make it the new tail. A tail pointer identifies the node to remove but not its predecessor, because links point only forward. Scanning from head is unavoidable with only these stored pointers. Reversing the operation orientation would allow constant-time deletion at head, but that is not this question’s data structure.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

Inserting at the head updates a constant number of pointers, Θ(1). Removing the tail requires locating its predecessor, which a singly linked list with only head/tail pointers does not directly supply; traversing n nodes costsΘ(n) in the worst case. Thus B.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text: Let ⊕ be XOR and ⊙ XNOR. Which identity is false? A ¬(P⊕Q)=P⊙Q; B (¬P)⊕Q=P⊙Q; C (¬P)⊕(¬Q)=P⊕Q; D (P⊕¬P)⊕Q=(P⊙¬P)⊙¬Q.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

XOR is 1 exactly when its inputs differ; XNOR is its complement. Complementing one input changes “different” to “equal”, proving B, while complementing both preserves whether they differ, proving C. In D simplify the inner gates first, rather than assuming associativity transfers between XOR and XNOR. A concrete counterexample is Q=0: the left evaluates to 1 and the right to 0, regardless of P.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

In D, P XOR not-P=1, so the left side is not-Q. Meanwhile P XNOR not-P=0, and 0 XNOR not-Q=Q. The sides are opposite, so D is false. Complementing a single XOR input gives XNOR, while complementing both leaves XOR unchanged, validating the other identities.

question_text: Which characterize conventional RISC design? I arithmetic only register-to-register; II fixed-length instructions; III hardwired control. Choices: A I,II; B II,III; C I,III; D all three.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

A load/store design keeps arithmetic operands in registers and uses separate instructions for memory transfers. Regular instruction lengths simplify fetching and decoding, while simple instruction semantics support direct hardwired control instead of a large microprogram. These properties work together to simplify pipelining. The question asks about the conventional design model; modern instruction-set families can have compressed encodings or other extensions without making the textbook characterization invalid.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

The conventional RISC design combines register-to-register arithmetic, fixed-length instruction encoding and hardwired control. All three listed characteristics apply, D. These are textbook design characteristics, not a claim that every modern RISC extension has identical instruction lengths.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: An NFA has n states. Its equivalent minimal DFA has k states. Which is always true? A k≥2^n; B k≥n; C k≤n²; D k≤2^n.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

A DFA must remember the entire set of NFA states that could currently be active. There are 2^n subsets of an n-element set. Some subsets may be unreachable and some reachable ones may be equivalent, so both reachability pruning and minimization can reduce this bound. There is no general lower bound k≥n: an NFA can contain many redundant states while accepting a language recognized by one DFA state. Some NFA families require exponentially many DFA states, ruling out a universal quadratic bound.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

Subset construction represents each DFA state by a subset of the NFA’s n states, so at most2^n states are needed, including a possible empty subset. Minimization cannot increase that count. Thus k≤2^n, D.

source_numbering_note: Normalized ordinal 17; source prints CS 7
subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: For recursively enumerable languages, choose the true statement: A closed under complement; B closed under intersection; C all are recursive; D there are uncountably many.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

A recognizer may run forever when the input is not in its language. For intersection, sequential simulation is sufficient: run the first recognizer and, if it accepts, run the second and accept only if it also accepts. An input in both languages reaches both acceptances; if the first simulation loops, that input is outside the intersection, where looping is permitted. Dovetailing is another valid construction, not a requirement here. Unlike intersection, union requires avoiding a loop in one recognizer that hides acceptance by the other. Finite machine descriptions are countable, and recognizable but undecidable languages refute C.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

To recognize the intersection of two recursively enumerable languages, dovetail their recognizers on the same input and accept when both accept. Hence intersection closure holds. Complement closure would make every recognizable language decidable, which is false; encodings of recognizers are countable. Thus B.

question_text: Choose the false claim: A CFGs can specify lexical and syntactic rules; B type checking precedes parsing; C high-level code can translate to different intermediate representations; D function arguments can be passed on the program stack.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

Parsing identifies constructs such as expressions, declarations and function calls. Type checking applies rules to those constructs and their symbol-table information, so the conventional dependency is syntax before semantic type checking. A compiler may interleave actions during parsing, but that does not establish the blanket claim in B. Regular token languages are also context-free, which is why A is expressively valid even though practical lexers usually use regular expressions.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

Parsing supplies the syntactic structure on which conventional type checking operates, so saying type checking is performed before parsing is false, B. CFGs can express regular lexical rules as well as syntax, multiple intermediate representations are possible, and stack argument passing is standard.

solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

At an instruction boundary the processor has a consistent state to save. Save that state before replacing the program counter, otherwise the return address and other status could be lost. Loading the interrupt-vector target transfers control to the handler; restoring saved state is meaningful only after the handler finishes. The model describes an ordinary precise interrupt, not an exception that aborts and restarts the current instruction.

Complete the current instruction(Q), save the interrupted process state(P), load the ISR entry PC(T), run the ISR(R), and restore the saved state(S). The order is QPTRS, A.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: A memory access costs M when resident and total D when it faults. Observed mean is X. Find fault rate: A (D−M)/(X−M); B (X−M)/(D−M); C (D−X)/(D−M); D (X−M)/(D−X).
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

Partition accesses into the two mutually exclusive outcomes. With fault probability f, their probabilities are f and 1−f, not two independent rates. The weighted mean X=M+f(D−M) interpolates between M at f=0 and D at f=1. These endpoints immediately distinguish the fault probability from C, which is the hit probability. For ordinary D>M, valid observations satisfy M≤X≤D.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

If f is the fault rate, X=(1−f)M+fD=M+f(D−M). Therefore f=(X−M)/(D−M), B, assuming the stated fault access time D is the total fault-case time and D≠M.

question_text: R is a many-to-one relation E1→E2. Both entity sets participate totally and |E1|>|E2|. Which holds? A each E1 entity has exactly one E2 partner; B some E1 entity has multiple E2 partners; C each E2 entity has exactly one E1 partner; D each E2 entity has at most one E1 partner.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

Treat the relation as a mapping from E1 into E2. “Many-to-one” imposes an upper bound of one on each E1 entity’s partners, and “total participation” imposes a lower bound of one. Together they force exactly one. On the E2 side total participation makes the map surjective, while the larger source cardinality invokes the pigeonhole principle: at least one E2 entity receives two or more partners.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

Many-to-one permits at most one E2 target per E1 entity. Total participation of E1 supplies at least one, hence exactly one. Total participation of E2 and |E1|>|E2| ensure some E2 target has multiple preimages, not exactly one each. Thus A.

question_text: For Book(isbn,bname) and Stock(isbn,copies), all queries select B.isbn,S.copies and join on equal isbn. Queries 1–4 respectively use INNER, LEFT OUTER, RIGHT OUTER and FULL OUTER JOIN. Which result necessarily contains the other three? A 1; B 2; C 3; D 4.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

Divide possible output rows into matched pairs, unmatched Book rows and unmatched Stock rows. An inner join emits only the first group. A left join additionally emits unmatched Book rows with null Stock columns; a right join analogously preserves unmatched Stock rows. A full join includes all three groups. Even after the common projection, every row generated by a narrower join still occurs in the full join, with at least the same multiplicity.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

The full outer join includes every matched pair plus all unmatched rows from each side padded by nulls. The inner and either one-sided outer join produce subsets of those rows after the same projection. Thus Query4, D; this remains a superset under SQL bag multiplicities.

question_text: During textbook slow start consider: i cwnd increases by 2 MSS per ACK; ii doubles per ACK; iii increases by 1 MSS per RTT; iv approximately doubles per RTT. Choose A ii,iii; B i,iii; C iv only; D i,iv.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

Suppose cwnd is w MSS at the start of a round, so approximately w full segments are sent. Each successful ACK adds roughly one MSS, and the w acknowledgments add w MSS in total. The next round therefore starts near 2w MSS. This is exponential growth by rounds, not by individual ACKs. A one-MSS increase per RTT describes the rough congestion-avoidance behavior instead of slow start.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

In textbook slow start, each ACK increases cwnd by approximately one MSS. With one ACK per segment in a full window, one RTT supplies about cwnd/MSS ACKs, approximately doubling the window. Only iv is true, C. Delayed ACKs and implementation details qualify the approximate doubling.

question_text: Each of two players independently rolls a fair six-faced die per trial; ties cause a retry. Find the probability that the game first has a winner on trial 3, rounded to three decimals.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

Of the 36 equally likely ordered roll pairs, six are ties: (1,1) through (6,6). The other 30 yield a winner, regardless of which player wins. To reach trial 3, the first two trials must both tie; the third must be non-tied. Independence permits multiplying these three probabilities. Do not multiply by an extra factor 2 for the two players: the decisive probability already includes both possible winners.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

A trial ties with probability6/36=1/6 and is decisive with probability5/6. Winning first on trial3 requires two ties then a decisive roll, probability(1/6)²(5/6)=5/216≈0.023148, rounded0.023.

question_text: Let u=(1,2)^T, v=(1,1)^T and A=uv^T. Find the largest eigenvalue.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

Write out the matrix to make the outer-product order explicit: A=[[1,1],[2,2]]. Its characteristic polynomial is (1−λ)(2−λ)−2=λ²−3λ=λ(λ−3), giving eigenvalues 0 and 3. This independently confirms the rank-one shortcut below. The scalar v^Tu is not the same matrix as uv^T; it supplies the nonzero eigenvalue because applying A to u returns a scalar multiple of u.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

A=uv^T has rank1. Its nonzero eigenvalue is v^Tu=1+2=3, since Au=u(v^Tu)=3u. The other eigenvalue is 0, so the largest is 3.

question_text: The undirected graph has vertices a,b,c,d,e,f and edges ab, ac, ae, bc, bd, bf, cd, ce, df, ef. Find its chromatic number.

A coloring result needs both a lower bound and a construction meeting it. The cycle a–b–c–a is a triangle, whose mutually adjacent vertices demand three different colors. Vertices a, b, c form a triangle, so at least3 colors are necessary. A valid3-coloring is{a, d}, {b, e}, {c, f}; every edge in the visually checked diagram joins different classes. Thus the chromatic number is 3.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: A finite group has 84 elements. What is the largest possible order of a proper subgroup?
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

For H≤G, cosets partition G into equally sized sets, so |G|=[G:H]|H|. Properness means index [G:H]≥2, hence |H|≤42. To show that the upper bound is possible rather than just necessary, use the cyclic group of order 84: its subgroup generated by the square of a generator has order 84/gcd(84,2)=42. The word “possible” matters because Lagrange’s divisibility condition does not generally guarantee a subgroup for every divisor in every group.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

Lagrange’s theorem requires a subgroup order to divide84. The greatest proper divisor is 42, and this is achievable in the cyclic group C84. Thus the largest possible order is 42. This is an attainable bound over groups of order84, not a guarantee that every such group has a subgroup of order42.

Postorder ends with the root, and inorder splits each subtree into left part, root, right part. Root 1 splits off right leaf 3. subject: 03-programming-in-c
question_text: Global int counter starts at 0. calc(a,b) increments counter, returns a*a*a if b==3, otherwise sets c=calc(a,b/3) and returns c*c*c. main calls calc(4,81), discards its return, then prints counter. Find the intended output.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

Count activations on the descent separately from arithmetic on the return path. Calls occur at b=81,27,9,3; the last still increments counter before testing the base case. Unwinding produces mathematical values 4³,4⁹,4²⁷,4⁸¹. Already 4²⁷=2^54 exceeds a signed 32-bit range, and the final 2^162 exceeds signed 64-bit range. Thus counting gives the intended answer, but actual C execution is not guaranteed once signed overflow occurs.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

The b arguments are81, 27, 9, 3, so counter is incremented four times before the base return. The intended answer is 4. However the return computation then cubes repeatedly to 4^81=2^162, overflowing signed int on ordinary32-bit or64-bit implementations. Signed overflow is undefined behavior in C even if main discards the return value, so the printed result is not portable without sufficiently wide integer arithmetic or an explicit abstraction that ignores overflow.

question_text: Two positive-edge D flip-flops share a clock. External in feeds D1; Q1 feeds D2; output is Q2. How many states have a transition to themselves for at least one input?
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

Both flip-flops sample their inputs at the same edge, so Q2 receives the old Q1, not the newly sampled input. With states written q1q2, input 0/1 transitions are: 00→00/10; 01→00/10; 10→01/11; 11→01/11. Only 00 and 11 appear among their own successors. This explicit table also shows why the mixed states cannot remain unchanged for either input.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

Let the state be(q1, q2). On a positive clock edge the next state is(in, q1), because both flip-flops sample old values simultaneously. A self-loop requires in=q1=q2, possible only for00 with input0 and 11 with input1. Exactly2 states have self-loops.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: A 1 GB, 32-bit-wide memory uses 256M×4-bit DRAMs. Each chip has 2^14 rows; refreshing a row takes 50 ns and all rows must refresh every 2 ms. Find the nearest-integer percentage available for reads/writes.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

Eight 4-bit chips operate in parallel to provide the 32-bit word. Since corresponding rows refresh together, the memory loses 16384 row-refresh slots per period, not eight times that number. Convert all durations to one unit: 2 ms=2000000 ns, and refresh consumes 819200 ns. Available time is 1180800 ns per period. Divide available time by total time, rather than reporting the refresh fraction.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

The row refresh time per period is 2^14·50 ns=819200 ns=0.8192ms. The remaining fraction of the 2ms period is 1−0.8192/2=0.5904, or59.04%, rounded59%. The eight parallel4-bit chips refresh a row together to form the 32-bit memory; their refresh times are not added serially.

source_numbering_note: Normalized ordinal 34; source prints CS 24
subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: Three processes share four identical resource instances. Each can need at most K, requesting and releasing one at a time. Find the largest K guaranteeing no deadlock.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

If every unfinished process has fewer than its maximum requirement, each may hold at most K−1 while waiting for another instance. With K=2, three such waiting processes can hold at most three resources, leaving the fourth available to let one finish. Releasing its resources then enables the others. For K=3, a feasible allocation (2,1,1) consumes all resources while each process can still request one; no request can be granted. This supplies both safety and a tight counterexample.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

For n=3 processes each requiring at most K identical resources, a sufficient and tight universal bound is R≥n(K−1)+1: for K=2, any allocation in which all three processes still need another instance leaves at least one of the four resources free; for K=3 the allocation (2,1,1) can instead exhaust all resources with all processes waiting. With R=4, K=2 satisfies4≥4, while K=3 permits holdings2, 1, 1 and all waiting. Thus the largest guaranteed-safe K is 2, assuming completed processes release their resources.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: A long-lived TCP connection sends at 10^9 bits/s and starts at sequence number 1234. Find the minimum time in seconds before that number can recur, rounded to an integer.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

A TCP sequence number labels a byte, so a full modulo-2^32 cycle consumes 4294967296 bytes, or 34359738368 bits. Divide by the bit rate, maintaining consistent units. The initial value 1234 affects which label comes first, but not how many increments return to it. This is a sequence-space throughput calculation; it does not independently establish that reusing the number is safe from delayed old packets.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

TCP sequence numbers count bytes modulo2^32. At10^9 bits/s, consuming the full sequence space requires2^32·8/10^9≈34.359738 seconds, rounded34. The starting number1234 only shifts the cycle and does not change its length.

subject: excluded
question_text: A 2×2 matrix P has only eigenvectors parallel to (1,4)^T. Which statements are necessary? I P is singular; II its eigenvalue repeats; III P is not diagonalizable. A I,III; B II only; C I,II; D II,III.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

Diagonalization in dimension two requires a basis of two linearly independent eigenvectors; the given one-dimensional eigenspace cannot provide it. Distinct eigenvalues would yield independent eigenvectors, so they must coincide. Repeated does not mean zero: take S=[[1,0],[4,1]] and J=[[1,1],[0,1]]. Then SJS^−1=[[-3,1],[-16,5]] has determinant 1, while its eigenvectors satisfy y=4x. This explicit nonsingular example refutes I.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

A2×2 matrix with only one eigenvector direction cannot be diagonalized, proving III. Two distinct eigenvalues would supply independent eigenvectors, so its eigenvalue must be repeated, II. Invertibility is not ruled out: any similarity transform of the nonsingular Jordan block [[1, 1],[0, 1]] with its first basis vector(1, 4) has exactly that eigenvector direction. Thus II and III, D.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: Let P be the rationals; Q the functions {0,1}→N; R the functions N→{0,1}; S the finite subsets of N. Which are countable? A Q,S; B P,S; C P,R; D P,Q,S.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

A function on two inputs is completely specified by the pair (f(0),f(1)), so Q is in bijection with N² and can be enumerated diagonally. A finite subset can be written as an increasing finite tuple; for each length these tuples are countable, and there are countably many lengths. In contrast a function in R specifies an infinite binary sequence. Cantor diagonalization constructs a sequence differing from the nth listed sequence at position n, defeating any proposed enumeration.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

Rationals are countable. Functions from{0, 1} to N correspond to ordered pairs of naturals, a countable set. Finite subsets of N are a countable union over subset size of countable collections. Functions N→{0, 1} correspond to arbitrary subsets of N and are uncountable by Cantor’s theorem. Thus P, Q, S, D.

question_text: A sentence ∃s∃t∃u∀v∀w∀x∀y ψ uses only predicate symbols and possibly equality, no functions; ψ is quantifier-free. It has a seven-element model. Which follows? A a model of size at most 3 exists; B no such small model exists; C no model larger than 7 exists; D every model has size 7.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

Choose the actual elements witnessing s,t,u in the given model; they need not be distinct. Use their set as a new nonempty universe and restrict each relation to tuples in that set. Atomic relations and equality on those elements retain exactly the same truth values. Boolean combinations, including negations, therefore retain their values too. Every assignment of universal variables in the smaller universe was already allowed in the original model, so the universal condition remains true.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

Take witnesses s, t, u in the supplied7-element model, and restrict the relational structure to those witnesses, at most3 distinct elements. With no functions or constants to require closure, atomic predicate and equality truth on retained tuples is unchanged, hence so is every quantifier-free combination ψ. Its universal assertions still hold for the restricted domain. The same witnesses therefore yield a model of size≤3, A.

subject: 03-programming-in-c
question_text: In C, str1="Hi", str2="Bye". fun1(char *s1,char *s2) swaps its local pointer variables using a temporary. fun2(char **s1,char **s2) swaps *s1 and *s2. main calls fun1(str1,str2), prints both strings, calls fun2(&str1,&str2), then prints both. Choices A Hi Bye Bye Hi; B Hi Bye Hi Bye; C Bye Hi Hi Bye; D Bye Hi Bye Hi.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

C passes arguments by value in both calls. In fun1 the copied values happen to be addresses of characters, so replacing those local copies cannot replace main’s variables. In fun2 the copied values are addresses of main’s pointer variables; dereferencing them selects those actual variables, which the assignments can modify. Neither routine edits the string literals. This distinction is between swapping pointed-to pointers and swapping local pointer copies, not between two language-level parameter-passing modes.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

fun1 swaps only local copies of the pointer values, leaving main’s strings unchanged: Hi Bye. fun2 receives their addresses and swaps the actual pointer variables, so the second output is Bye Hi. The whole output is Hi Bye Bye Hi, A.

source_numbering_note: Normalized ordinal 40; source prints CS 30
subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: For a simple undirected graph, I says DFS has no cross edge between unrelated vertices; II says every graph edge joins BFS depths differing by exactly 1. Which must hold? A I only; B II only; C both; D neither.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

If an undirected DFS edge led to a still-unvisited vertex, DFS would explore it before returning, making that vertex a descendant. If the vertex is already on the recursion stack it is an ancestor; an edge to a completed unrelated subtree would have discovered the current vertex earlier. For BFS, shortest-path distances differ by at most 1 across an edge. A triangle rooted at one vertex places the other two at depth 1 and still has an edge between them, disproving “exactly”.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

In undirected DFS, an edge to an undiscovered vertex is explored before the current DFS call completes, so every non-tree edge joins an ancestor and descendant; no cross edges, making I true. BFS edges can connect equal-depth vertices, for example the edge joining the two non-root vertices of a triangle. The necessary inequality is |i−j|≤1, not equality1. Thus only I, A.

solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

The dynamic-programming state M[i,j] is the minimum scalar cost of multiplying the consecutive subchain; a split k adds the costs of its two subchains and their final product. This systematically tests all parenthesizations without a local greedy assumption. In the winning chain, F3F4 first produces 3×1 at cost 48; F2 times that gives 25×1 at cost 75; F1 times that gives 2×1 at cost 50; multiplying F5 costs 2000. Only the first operation multiplies two original matrices directly.

Use matrix-chain DP: M[i, j]=min_k(M[i, k]+M[k+1, j]+d[i−1]d[k]d[j]). Dimensions are2, 25, 3, 16, 1, 1000. question_text: Physical addresses span 2^P bytes, words have 2^W bytes, cache capacity is 2^N bytes, blocks hold 2^M words, and associativity is K. Choose tag bits: A P−N−log₂K; B P−N+log₂K; C P−N−M−W−log₂K; D P−N−M−W+log₂K.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

A byte address has P bits. First convert block capacity from words to bytes, obtaining 2^(M+W). Cache blocks total 2^(N−M−W); grouping K per set divides this by K. Address bits split into tag, set index and byte-within-block offset. Increasing associativity at fixed capacity reduces index bits and therefore increases tag bits, a useful sign check on the log₂K term. The result assumes integral power-of-two field sizes.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

A block contains2^(M+W) bytes. There are2^(N−M−W)/K sets, so index bits=N−M−W−log2K, and block-offset bits=M+W. Subtract both from P address bits: tag=P−N+log2K, B, under the conventional power-of-two cache parameters.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: Over words a^m b^n c^p d^q, with all exponents nonnegative, define I m+p=n+q; II m=n and p=q; III m=n=p and p≠q; IV mn=p+q. Which are context-free? A I,IV; B I,II; C II,III; D II,IV.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

One stack can track a single signed difference, so the crossed-looking equality in I is still manageable; a finite-state component checks block order. II has grammar S→AB, A→aAb|ε, B→cBd|ε. For III, restricting to positive a,b,c blocks and no d leaves the standard non-CFL equal-three-count language. For IV, the multiplication constraint cannot be reduced to one additive counter. The pumping argument below makes this precise, including decompositions that cross a block boundary rather than assuming where the pumped substrings lie.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

I is context-free: a PDA tracks the signed running difference(#a+#c)−(#b+#d) with one stack symbol for positive excess and another for negative excess, canceling opposite contributions; finite control enforces a*b*c*d* order. II is the concatenation{a^n b^n}{c^p d^p}, a CFL. For III, intersect with a+b+c+ (no d); the result is{a^n b^n c^n: n≥1}, not context-free. For IV, suppose pumping length p and take a^p b^p c^(p²). subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: Classify: I membership w∈L(G) for unrestricted G; II whether a TM language is regular; III equality of languages of two unrestricted/general grammars; IV whether an NFA language has an equivalent deterministic PDA. Options A only I,II undecidable; B only III; C only II,IV; D only I,II,III.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

Rice’s theorem applies to nontrivial properties of the recognized language, not to arbitrary syntactic machine properties. Regularity is nontrivial because some recognizable languages are regular and some are not. Equivalence of general grammars includes comparing a grammar to one generating the empty language, already an undecidable emptiness problem. IV is different: every regular language has a DFA, and a deterministic PDA can simulate a DFA while leaving its stack unchanged. Therefore IV is a constant-yes decision problem.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

I is the undecidable membership problem for unrestricted grammars/Turing-recognizable languages. II is a nontrivial semantic property of a TM language, hence undecidable by Rice’s theorem. III, equivalence of general grammars, is undecidable (even equivalence of CFGs is undecidable). IV always has answer yes: convert the NFA to a DFA and view that DFA as a DPDA that does not use its stack. Hence only I, II, III are undecidable, D. If III were restricted to regular grammars it would be decidable, but no such restriction is stated.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text: Tokens are T1=a?(b|c)*a, T2=b?(a|c)*b, T3=c?(b|a)*c, where ? is optional. Scan bbaacabc using longest-prefix matching. Choices A T1,T2,T3; B T1,T1,T3; C T2,T1,T3; D T3,T3.
question_text_status: self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and choices; not verbatim; original wording/figures remain at source_url
solution:
Method and intermediate reasoning:

At the first position T1 can consume bba: its final a ends the token before the next a. T2 can consume bb but cannot include both leading b symbols in its middle (a|c)*. T3 consumes bbaac; it cannot consume the entire input because its middle cannot contain the earlier c. Remove that five-character prefix and rescan abc, which T3 consumes completely. Longest match is decided afresh at each position, rather than choosing the earliest token pattern that can match anything.

Derivation, answer and qualifications:

On bbaacabc, the longest first token is bbaac, matching T3=(optional c)(a|b)*c. T1 matches only bba and T2 only bb at that position. The remaining abc also matches T3 in full, longer than the alternatives. Therefore the output is T3, T3, D.
